other_info: 2 full-page vellum diagrams (one retaining its moveable volvelle, the other apparently without), one quadrans drawn on vellum, 10 full-page illustrations of eclipses (for the time period 1475-1530);                                  including significant portions of Regiomontanus' Kalendarium together with other prognostic texts. other_info: Decoration includes 6 full-page miniatures. All of the miniatures appear to be of the Ferrara-Bologna school represented by Costa and Aspertini. Bernard Berenson ascribes the St. Jerome to an unknown pupil of Costa influenced by Ercole Roberti; he thinks that the portrait of Giovanni II Bentivoglio may be by Amico Aspertini in his earlier years; the David is possibly by Costa himself; while the Christ Child adored by the Virgin and St. George, and St. George slaying the dragon, are by Tamaroccio. In Mr. Berenson's opinion the Crucifixion is by a painter close to both Costa and Francia, who may have been Chiodarolo in his earlier years. Girolamo Pagliarolo, who signed and dated the manuscript in 1497, can be credited with the elaborate border ornament as well as the writing. Emblems and arms of Bentivoglio, Gonzaga, and Manfredi are repeated throughout.

other_info: An elegant compilation of Latin elegiac poetry written in Renaissance Bologna. Little is known of the 6th-century Latin poet Maximianus, save for what can be inferred from his poetry – his claim to be of Etruscan descent means he is sometimes referred to as ‘Maximianus Etruscus’ – and scholars dispute whether his verses can be securely attributed to a single author. His Elegies were part of the teaching corpus in the 11th and 12th centuries; they appeared in printed editions of the 15th century, before the 1501 edition by Pomponius Gauricus misattributed his verse to the first-century-BC poet Cornelius Gallus, an error which persisted in print for hundreds of years. The elegiac poem Nux is among the corpus of works whose authorship is credited to Ovid in the manuscript tradition but not by modern scholars, hence: ‘Pseudo-Ovid’. Our manuscript is referenced in Martin Pulbrook's edition of the Nux poem (Maynooth, 1985, pp. 13, 66-71).

other_info:
Ruled space: c.235 x 70mm, catchwords survive, running headers throughout in blue and red, rubrics in red, paraph marks alternately blue and red, initials alternately blue and red with penwork flourishing in red or blue, 4 full-height illuminated bar borders, 68 historiated initials, of which 6 with full-length human figures, 14 with mythical creatures, a marriage scene, a murder, and the rest with profiles of men, women, nobles and monks, 90 foliate initials (initials on ff.2 and 257 rubbed, some leaves yellowed, a few holes, natural flaws and contemporary stitched repairs, a few creases, else in excellent condition). 

The style of illumination is typical of Bolognese workshops of the beginning of the 14th century: features are highlighted in white, contours of faces are heavily shaded and brows are decisively rendered. There are strong similarities with the work of the Bolognese workshop that executed a Bible in Bologna (Collegio di Spagna, MS 2), as well as a Breviary at the Morgan Library, MS M.0373.

titles: Gregory I, Saint and Pope, Dialogi de vita et miraculis patrum Italicorum; Bonaventura. Legenda Minor and Legenda Maior of the Life of St Francis
authors: Gregory I, Pope, c. 540-604 (Gregory I, Saint and Pope); Bonaventure, Saint, Cardinal, c. 1217-1274 (Bonaventura)
places: Bologna, Emilia-Romagna, Northern Italy, Italy, Europe; Padua, Veneto, Northern Italy, Italy, Europe
manuscript_binding: Late fourteenth or early fifteenth century brown calf over wooden boards (see comments for more info)
other_info:
2 works in one vol., illuminated manuscript on vellum, 70 leaves (with 2 added paper leaves, and 4 old parchment flyleaves), quires numbered throughout on first and last leaf: I-II12 (a paper leaf, numbered 27, loosely between second and third quire, which belongs after fol. 42), III14+3 (three paper leaves, including fol. 27, added after third quire with chapter indices added perhaps in the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century), IV 12, V8, VI12 , last leaf closing with "omnis isti quaternii sunt", modern pencil foliation in upper right including the flyleaves (thus starting with no. 3 on the first leaf of the book), text in Latin, ruled in plummet for 38 or 39 lines in two columns (50 or 51 lines per page from fol. 64), justification 125 x 85mm. and 116 x 87mm., written in light brown ink in a Southern Semi-Textualis Libraria (cf. Derolez 2003, pl. 55), some later modifications (probably fifteenth century) in black ink (e.g. fol. 1), rubrics in red, versals touched in red, red and blue paragraph marks, red and blue lombards at the beginning, two-line and one nine-line initials in red and blue with blue and red penwork throughout, FIVE ILLUMINATED INITIALS introducing each book, in varying colours on golden burnished grounds with figurated extensions towards lower margins, the extensions including one or two medallions with bust- or full portraits, the illuminations slightly flaked and rubbed, prickings all preserved, three wormholes to the last leaves, late fourteenth or early fifteenth century brown calf over wooden boards, blind tooled with geometric lines in diamond pattern, four small round stamps in the corners of front and back covers, sewn on five throngs, pastedowns removed? from the boards to serve as two of the four manuscript flyleaves, restoration to traces of a now missing clasp, some loss to spine.
Contents:
(ignoring pencil foliation)
Fol. 1-59v: Incipit: "Incipiunt capitula primi libri dialigorum beati gregorii papae", explicit: "...et fidentes dico que salutatis hostia ipsi fuerimus"; a later hand has added "Explicit liber dialogorum beati gregorii pape deo gratias Amen".
Fol. 60: Probably originally blank, with a list of sacraments, the celestial order, vices and virtues.
Fol. 60v-61: Probably originally blank, with a treatise on paradise and a meditation on the cross, most likely added in the fifteenth century.
Fol. 61v: in a hand contemporary to the main text: List of prayers to be addressed to various saints in order to receive a certain number of indulgences from various popes.
Fol. 62-70v: Bonaventura de Bagnoregio's Legenda Minor Sancti Francisci, followed by the more exhaustive Legenda Maior Sancti Francisci. Incipit: "Apparuit gratia dei salvatoris nostri diebus istis novissimis ..."; Explicit: "Quo nos introducat verus populi ductor et Salvator, Christus Iesus crucifixus, per merita servi sui Francisci, ad laudem et gloriam unius Dei et trini, qui vivit et regnat in saecula saeculorum. Amen".
Provenance:
1. The illumination and some contemporary amendments to the text suggest that the book was made for a convent of the Friars Minor, most likely of the Franciscan order in the Emilia Romagna.
2. The manuscript was newly bound in the early fifteenth century as indicated by the added paper. Fol. 25 has a text insertion which starts "Incipit testamentum quod fecit beatissimus pater nostrum Sanctus Franciscus propter obitum suum ..."; this, along with another added paragraph on St. Nicholas on fol. 27, indicates that the manuscript must have been part of a Franciscan library in the fifteenth century, where it was kept up to date.
3. Round ink stamp with the initials 'FRC' on the second front flyleaf, later nineteenth or early twentieth century.

other_info:
SIGNED AND DATED BY THE SCRIBE FRANCONIS DE GHEELE, manuscript on paper, 257 leaves (and 2 modern flyleaves), quires of ten except XV (six) and XXVI (ten plus one), text in Latin, ruled in plummet for 60 lines in two columns, justification 257 x 175mm., intercolumnal space approximately 38mm., written in light brown ink in a Flemish looking Textualis Libraria by two hands (first hand: fols. 1-144, first book; second hand: fols. 147-257, second book), catchwords preserved throughout, distinctive five-line paragraph headings, decorated throughout with red and blue paragraph marks, two- to eight-line initials in red and blue with elaborate red and purple penwork, 2 LAVISHLY ILLUMINATED INITIALS WITH BURNISHED GOLD and spiralling acanthus leaves in red, blue, green and mauve highlighted with white penwork to open each of the two books, first leaf with coat of arms, one of the watermarks (e.g. fol. 47) a six-pointed star (very similar to Piccard no. 41614 in a manuscript in Innsbruck), the other a striding dog without collar (not listed in Piccard or the watermark database), wide margins, modern pencil foliation in upper right including on flyleaves, an irregular older ink foliation in lower right with higher numbers, first page darkened and thumbed, illuminated initial with some waterstains and flaking of burnished gold, second illuminated initial bright and very fresh, fold of first leaf strengthened with paper, some waterstaining, mostly in margins, text slightly affected in places but remaining legible at all times, a few leaves strengthened and restored (usually towards centre of quire to protect paper from the thread), many contemporary comments and small drawings of faces and manicula in margins, careful corrections of mistakes, blindstamp in lower blank margin of 2 leaves, eighteenth century red morocco gilt, spine lettered in gilt "Ius canoni/Manuscrip/A. Samsone de Gheele/Anno MCCCXXXVI", g.e. folio (382 x 278mm.), Italy, [Bologna or Padua(?), signed and dated by the scribe Franconis de Gheele, 21 June, 1436]
Provenance:
1. The original coat of arms of the first unidentified owner, in the lower margin of the first page, has been overpainted. As can be judged from the verso of this leaf, the coat of arms must have been a diagonal yellow/golden bar over a multicoloured shield (red, white and green?).
2. Later in the fifteenth century the manuscript seems to have been used by legal scholars. There are many annotations and drawings of coats of arms in the margins, probably referring to duchies or members of the nobility to whom certain laws might apply, and a detailed index following the first book was added around the same time.
3. The eighteenth century owner, who had the manuscript rebound, seems to have overpainted the original coat of arms with his own, an overturned sun with a face and spreading rays on a red ground, with a blue band and three white stars above.
4. M. Jean Baptiste Théodore de Jonghe of Gent (1801-1860), one of the most notable bibliophiles of his time, with his bookplate.
5. Brussels, F. Heussner, Livres et manuscrits formant la Bibliothèque de Feu M.J.B.TH. de Jonghe, Officier de l'ordre de Léopold, 9 November 1860, vol. 1, lot 172/f1564.
6. Purchased from Sotheran and Co., September 1900 (note on fly-leaf).

other_info: [Note: all manuscripts from the catalogue from the City Library (Ville. Cod.) were destroyed in the 17 May, 1940 firebombing of Tournai except those that have a current shelfmark noted in the Current Location field. The incomplete catalogue of the City Library represents the efforts of Paul Faider to catalogue the collection in the lead-up to its destruction, and includes only 170 of the 247 MSS it held at that time. See original catalogue for very detailed descriptions of MSS and contents; the notes here summarize.] These questions were often printed in Venice in the 15th and 16th centuries [see bibliography in original catalogue]. Volume presents the typical characteristics of university manuscripts from the north of Italy (Bologne or Padua?). The beginning of books is marked by gilt and ornamented initials in the Italian style; signing of each gathering with a letter on the recto of the first leaf; gatherings of 10, the first 5 signed on recto and with a catchword on the last. The hand is careful and regular, but the ink has yellowed and faded. Running headers. Precise corrections. Quite a few glosses. On the front board and on the 3 flyleaves (3v blank), glosses introduced by a nota and a reference to a questio from the text. On the rear board, a four-line note almost entirely erased: [...] p[ro] p[res]tio x ducat [...] t[em]p[or]e quo eram [...] philosophie [...] anno d[omi]ni 1454. titles: Recueil de privileges de la ville de Cologne
other_info:
Supplement francais 4231.
1. Privileges (131 articles); incipit (fol. 1 v) : "In dem namen der heiliger dreiueldigheit und des waren Gottes... In dem beginn und anfang so als unsere liebe getreuwe freunde..." (fol. 1-68 r).
2. "Concordata des Ertzbischoffs und Churfursten des Reichs, weilche antreffen das Stift und die Stadt Coellenn" (fol. 68 v-79 v).
3. "Diese nachgeschrieben puncten seint loblicher stadt Coellen recht..." (fol. 80 r-85 v; fol. 86 blanc).
4. "Der verbundt brieff gemacht anno domini 1396" (fol. 87 r-fol 98 v).
5. "Transfix brieff" (fol. 99 r-110 v).
6. "Item der Ratsherren vnsererr Stadt Coellen Eidtbuch" (fol. 111 r-130 v).
7. "Item hernach folgt van den verordenten Erbschreinen" (fol. 131 r-142 r).
8. "Diese... puncten seint... van den Broitbecheren vnserer Stadt Coeln" (fol. 143 r-154 v; fol. 155, 156 en blanc).
9. Testament de Heinrich Haith, 4 juillet 1452 (fol. 157 r-162 v).
10. "Inhalt der beider Renthmeister Eidt" suivis des serments d'autres administrateurs, fol. 163 r-215 v).
11. "Die Rolle an dem gruene vischmart" (fol. 216 r-224 r).
12. Interrogatoires et sentences de Diederich Spitz et de ses complices (janvier 1513) (fol. 225-242; ecrit d'une autre main que le reste du manuscrit).
Fol. 1 porte l'inscription : Johan Wilhelm von der Rech.
provenance: Bibliothèque nationale de France

source_title: Catalogue des Manuscrits Allemands de la Bibliotheque Nationale [Revue des Bibliotheques 4, 1894, pp. 1-128 (G. Huet)]
titles: Recueil de pieces concernant la ville de Cologne
other_info:
Supplement francais, 4513.
Divided in 2 parts; each part has its own pagination.
1. Partie paginee, fol 1-38 : se divise en deux parties:
a : Fol. 1-2 et 1938 : recit d'une emeute en Cologne en 1482 (en vers); suivi (fol. 34 v-38 v) de la liste des bourgmestres depuis l'an 1396. Incipit (fol. 1 v) : "Van einem uplauff der geschiet ist In disser Statt Collen..." Publie dans les Chroniken der deutschen Staedte XIV, 946 ss.
b (insere dans la partie precedente, fol. 3-18; ecriture plus recente) edit sur les affaires de religion ("Morgenspraich anno 1609 publicirt") et pieces diverses.
2. Partie paginee fol. 1-210.
a : Serments de fonctionnaires et reglements divers, fol. 1-50; incipit: "Der Eidt den die Weinroeder thun sollen".
b : Accord entre la ville de Cologne et l'Archeveque (fol. 51-67); incipit : "Dit sint die Concordaten die tuischen dem Bischoff vnd der Statt Collen gemacht..."
c : Proclamation des magistrats sur les discordes dans la ville, fol. 68-69.
d : Entree du Roi des Romains a Cologne ("Roemscher Konninck Huldunge ") fol. 69-70, et entree d'un Archeveque (fol. 70), suivie d'autres formules, decisions relatives aux successions et testaments, droit penal, mesures de police, procedure (fol. 71-142 v, 143-145 blancs).
e : Proces de Diederich Spies et de ses complices (janvier 1513) (fol. 146-169).
f : "Ditt ist der Staith Coellen Recht vnd Burger Freiheit" (fol. 170-177.)
g : "Ditt is die Copey des Verbountbrieffs..." (fol. 178-191; "datum anno Domini millesimo trecentesimo nonagesimo sexto").
h: "Transfix Breve" (fol. 192-210). Explicit (fol. 210 v) "Beschlossen und verdragen im Jar unsers Herren 1513, auff den 15 tag des Monats decembris".
La partie fol. 170-210 est ecrite d'une autre main que le reste du manuscrit.
L'ex libris porte : "Ex bibliotheca L. B. de Belderbusch".
provenance: Bibliothèque nationale de France

Written in a Gothic bookhand, with numerous initials, running titles and paragraph marks in red and/or blue, six large floral initials in red and blue extending into the margin. The manuscript also includes a second different translation of 'De mystica theologia' and 'De divinis nominibus'.

Ravissant Manuscrit de 217 ff., écrit en lettres gothiques, en rouge et noir, réglé. [...] La miniature représente l' Annonciation, l'encadrement porte en bas les armes de la famille Pandolfini, soutenues par 2 putti, en haut le monogramme du Christ. Les autres petites miniatures renfermées dans des initiales, sont la Vierge et l'Enfant, dans la bordure Abraham, en médaillon, en bas des armoiries tenues par 2 anges; la Mort, dans la bordure, médaillon avec la figure d'un Saint; David avec sa harpe, dans la bordure médaillon, la tête de Goliath; la Croix, dans la bordure médaillon, le Christ avec les stigmes; l'Enfant Jésus, dans la bordure médaillon, Marie et S. Joseph. Les bordures décorées de rinceaux et fleurs, sont d'un beau style. Le tout est finement peint en vives couleurs et rehaussé d'or luisant. Dans le texte on rencontre une quantité de lettres ornées, dessinées à la plume en rouge et bleu, dont les arabesques s'étendent sur les marges. - Conférez l'article de Paolo D'Ancona, "di alcuni codici miniati di scuola fiorentina" in La Bibliofilia anno X, 1908-9, pp. 48-49. Les marges sont très larges et la conservation est excellent sauf les 2 premières miniatures qui sont tout légèrement fanées et piquées. authors: Petrarca, Francesco, 1304-1374 (Petrarca, Francesco) [Attr]; Dante Alighieri, 1265-1321 (Dante Allighieri di Fireenze) [Attr]
other_info: Written during the life-time of Petrarch, or immediately after his death, for Lorenzo the son of Carlo degli Strozzi (a member of one of the noblest families of Florence) by Paul the Scribe, as appears by the colophon: "Gratissimi spetiosique hujus voluminis adepto fiet Laus sit et Gloria Deo qui Laurentio Karoli de Stroccis qui ipsum fieri fecit Pauloque Scriptori ejusdem felicem tribuat vitam per tempora longiora. Amen"  The volume is adorned with large initial letters, and three illuminated borders, containing portraits of the Poets and their Inamoratas, executed in the style of Florentine art at that period, with the arms of the Strozzi emblazoned in the bottom compartment o the first two.  From the colophon in which Laurentius de Strozzis is called Filius Karoli without the quondam, the Beatae Memoriae, or any other formula t the same effect, which, no doubt, would have been used at that time in Italy, if Karolus was dead when that colophon was written, it is clear that he was still alive at that moment;  and, as this celebrated Florentine died at a very advances age in 1383, the volume was written before that time, but how long it is difficult to ascertain.  All we can say is, that Lorenzo (for whom this volume was written) had five sisters, who, as early as the year 1331, were all nuns in the monastery of St. Dominic at Florence (see Litta), and no doubt he had arrived at the age of manhood, and was quite able to collect fine books long before the year 1383.

other_info: Illuminated title-page with an embellished initial C. In the lower central medallion, the arms of Mathias Corvinus, King of Hungary, flanked by smaller circles bearing his emblems: a flint and steel, and a purse. The facing page gives the contents of the book in eleven numbered circles surrounding a large wreath, lettered in alternating lines of gold and blue. At the top, in the twelfth circle, is an armillary sphere, another emblem of the king. The manuscript also contains seven illuminated armorial incipit pages. The ornamental style reflects that of Antonio del Chierico. The text of Niccoli's 'Commentarium' is written by a different scribe. Originally written for a member of the Chyurlia di Lizzano family, whose arms remain in the border of f. 175.

The text, written in beautiful, well-spaced black and blue antica tonda script, has gold rubrics and initials on alternating blue and rose fields. Attavante's genius for lavish ornament and rich colour effects is exemplified throughout. In the centre of a lower border, the arms of the Di Domenico family of Florence appear. From the arms of the Pitti and Taddei de' Gaddi families which occur in various combinations, it appears that the prayer book was compiled for a descendant of Buonaccorso Pitti, whose son Rupert was married to Giovanna de' Taddei. The calendar, written in gold, stresses Milanese saints.

other_info: [clipping from catalogue LXXIII:] 3303. Avec 2 superbes bordures, 74 petites initiales historiées, 15 petites initiales ornem. et 43 pièces ornem. en bas des pages, le tout miniaturé par Francesco Antonio del Cherico. De plus une foule innombrable de lettrines de diverse dimension, avec des rinceaux, peintes en rouge et bleu. [...] [sale price:] 20,000 [French Francs] [...] Les ff. 1-6 contiennent le Calendrier. F. 7 r: INcipit ordo breuiarij fr. | trur minor secūdur cō- | suetudine romane cu- | rie.... Cette page est encadrée d'une riche bordure formée d'ornements, de rinceaux, de fleurs, d'oiseaux, de génies etc. jolie composition pleine d'une sérénité non commune. Aux extrémités et au milieu on voit 7 médaillons avec des scènes de la vie. de S. François, et dans le bas les armoiries d'un évêque. Le Psautier commence au ro du f. 201: INcipit plalterium. vm | nus iste filicet.... La page est encadrée d'une semblable bordure, renfermant 2 petites miniatures. F. 284 v les Hymnes et Offices, par lesquels se termine le manuscrit. Les 74 initiales historiées mesurent 23 X 23 à 26 mm. chacune et sur un espace si limité l'artiste a représenté des scènes inspirées par la Bible ou par la vie des martyrs, avec plusieurs personnages, tous très distinctement exécutés. L'expression des figures, le dessin artistique, le coloris délicat et vif démontrent l'infatigable fantaisie du maître. Les pièces ornementales, en bas des pages, sont formées do rinceaux, de fleurs, d'oiseaux et d'autres animaux, elles sont d'un style gracieux et très variées et portent au milieu une banderole avec une légende. Les innombrables lettrines, parsemées dans le texte, sont ornées d'arabesques et de rinceaux tirés en rouge et bleu. [...] Conférez l'intéressant article de Paolo D'Ancona dans la Revue "La Bibliofilía" anno X, disp. 2-3, 1908, pp. 45-48. other_info: "This memorandum book of a Florentine grain dealer contains entries made in a variety of hands, possibly those of the buyers, with entries for payment for grain, rent, taxes, alms, and other income. The number of entries for each year is small. This account book is characteristic of the type used when Palioli created his treatise on double entry bookkeeping. The book designates Biagio Dicino dalle Vanna as the official recorder of transactions and also mentions other members of his family. The entries are dated from 1466-1524, but leaves with entries for 1473-1475, 1495, and 1501-1503 are missing....Contemporary foliation in ink, upper right recto; 1-5, 7, 10-15, 17, 19-30, 35-44, 48-79, 81-94 (gaps due to missing leaves, except for a foliation error omitting 80)"

manuscript_binding: "Leather, blind-tooled and -stamped, with two clasps; Costumi, Cambi, Moneta, Pesi, written on spine in ink;"
other_info: "This manuscript is a fifteenth-century Italian compendium of practical information for Florentine merchants, including rules of exchange and a method for finding out what day of the week a given month begins in a given year. It is a humanistic manuscript on parchment. The work in this manuscript was published in Florence in December 1481; the colophon of the manuscript is dated July 1481. The body of the text follows closely the version in Paciola's later Summa de arithmetica, published in 1494. Most of the chapter numbers in the chapter headings of the manuscript, left blank by the scribe, were filled in by a later reader. The manuscript contains 195 chapters whereas the printed versions contain only 194 chapters....Six-line illuminated initial and damaged coat of arms surrounded by a laurel wreath and floral extensions on first page of text (fol. 9r); two-line and four-line red and blue initials throughout; rubrication in red" Colophon: "Finito libro isto referamus gratia Christo, die mensis Julii, MCCCCLXXXI, per me S[er?] Ludovicho Bertini"

other_info: ... dedicato "ad clarissimum virum Petrum Medicem magni Cosmae Fi.". La scena miniata più importante, che raffigura la prima delle nostre riproduzioni, si nota nell'ultima delle tre carte di guardia iniziali del manoscritto. Sul dinanzi campeggiano le figure di Annibale e di Scipione, alia testa di due respettive squadre di cavalieri, usciti fuori dagli attendamenti trincerati e pronti alia battaglia ... La seconda fotografia che pubblichiamo rende inutile una dettagliata scrizione dell'altra carta miniata di questo codicetto. L'ornamentazione di essa in nulla diversifica dal motivo divenuto consueto nelle carte iniziali dei manoscritti quattrocenteschi: lungo i quattro margini è il solito fregio a fio compreso fra liste dorate, ornato con mezze figurine entro medaglioni e formelle ovoidali ; nell'alto è espresso il titolo e la dedica del libro a caratteri rubricati aurei su fondo ceruleo ; in basso apresi lo stemma del possessore fra cornucopie graziosamente sorrette da alati puttini ignudi ...

source_title: New York 2016. Forty Books
titles: Rime e prose diverse (zibaldone); Acquattino; Sfera
manuscript_binding: 19th-century English gilt-tooled calf
other_info: Composite manuscript containing 52 differents texts (partially palimpsest, texts 5, 50-51, underlying texts in chancery cursive and rounded Gothic hand). Two world maps, one in T-form, the other with outlines of the Old World; 14 colored drawings, depicting the celestial spheres, zodiac, eclipses, and wind directions. A veritable treasure of unrecorded texts, a miscellaneous codex or zibaldone put together in the middle of the 15th century, and including a great variety of treatises, poems, letters, orations, and a few writings which date as early as 1327. Among the 52 different texts contained specially noteworthy is the Latin text of the decree issued by the Florentine Inquisition against the medieval astrologer and ‘heretic’ Cecco d’Ascoli, a remarkable discovery because until today the decree was known only in its Italian version, testified by later manuscripts. Equally of interest are a richly illustrated copy of the Sfera by Gregorio Dati; an exceptionally early text dating from the period of the Great Schism (ca. 1408) and purporting to be written by the Devil; a poem against sodomy composed by Giovanni da Prato, entitled Acquattino, i.e. the nickname adopted for the most famous figure here mentioned as a sodomite, the Florentine Giovanni Gherardi da Prato.
provenance: (Richard Heber); (Thomas Phillipps)

titles: Books of Hours, Use of Rome and the Carmelites (?), in Latin
manuscript_binding: Sewn on five cords, with endbands; bound in early 19th-c. English (?) brown leather over pasteboards, with onlays of red leather dotted in gilt; spine in seven compartments without bands; marbled endpapers conjoint with pastedowns; gilt edges [cat. pl. 1]
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly MS. Lat. liturg. e. 28. i (paper) + 196 + ii (paper). Modern foliation in pencil i, 1-41a, 41b-197. 23 quires mostly of 10, but with numerous leaves missing. Ruled in pale grey-blue ink (quires I-VIII, XIV-XX) and pale brown (remainder). Headed in red; guides to rubrics and colored initials in tiny cursive script; capitals touched in pale yellow wash. | Contents. Hours of the Virgin, Use of Rome (imperfect); Long Hours of the Cross (misbound and imperfect); Penitential Psalms (imperfect); Litany and collects; Office of the Dead, Carmelite (?) use (imperfect); Calendar, very sparse. | Decoration. Four seven-line historiated initials, each below a colored panel with the heading of the text, mostly in square capitals of the humanist style, surrounded by a four-sided border containing further scenes in panels framed in gold. 1r Hours of the Virgin, initial D[omine]: Virgin and Child, lower border with two putti flanking a coat of arms. 81r Hours of the Cross, initial D[omine]: Man of Sorrows, standing in the tomb; 109r Penitential Psalms, initial D[omine]: King David playing the psaltery [cat. pl. 23]; 130r Office of the Dead, initial D[ilexi]: half-length skeleton holding scythe, border in a different style from others with lush acanthus foliage. Four-line painted foliate initials with burnished and painted gold at the start of each hour from Prime to Compline in the Hours of the Virgin; similar three-line initials in to the same hours in the Hours of the Cross; three-line initials in gold with blue, or blue with red, respectively, to Lauds of the Hours of the Virgin and the Cross; two-line initials to psalms, lessons, KL monograms in the calendar, etc.; one-line initials alternately in gold or blue to verses and other minor textual divisions. Illumination attributed by Garzelli to Mariano del Buono di Jacopo. | Made for a member of the Florentine Bellacci family (?): their (?) coat of arms on 1r, vert, a bend argent, with three uncertain five-pointed objects gules, the shield within a wreath held by two putti; matches the Bellacci arms if the five-pointed objects represent cinquefoils or roses. The responses of the nine lessons of the Office of the Dead are assigned by Ottosen to a wide variety of places, mostly French, but also to Sarum and Carmelite uses; the latter is assigned here on acccount of the Bellacci family's Carmelite links. Subsequent provenance includes Adolphe Labitte, Paris bookseller; perhaps bought by Thomas Buchanan with MS Buchanan e. 5 and Buchanan e. 136 in October 1857.

source_title: A descriptive catalogue of the manuscripts in the library of Corpus Christi College Cambridge
titles: Historia ab inclinatione Romani imperii (Third Decade)
other_info:
Lib. ab Al. 2, T. James 378. Written a good Italic hand, on white vellum. It was in the collection (as we see from T. James) before 1600, but does not occur in Parker's list. Fol. i has a very fine full border of massive gold and colour, of characteristic Florentine work. Three times in the border occurs a blue shield with a representation of a barrel with a fire in it, set on an upright shaft upon a square base, and approached by a ladder. This is thought by George Williams, editor of the Correspondence of Bishop Bekynton (Rolls Series, I, xxxiii) to be the rebus of Th[omas] Bekynton (Beacon-tun), Bishop of Bath and Wells. Flavio Biondo (the author of the volume before us) was a correspondent of Bekynton's, and in a letter (I, p. 241) promises him a gift, which is probably this book. The letter in question was written at Florence in 1442. The initial has a half-length figure of a man in upright cylindrical red cap, and dark red robe, holding a book. 
This MS. contains the Third Decade of Fl. Blondus's 'Historia ab inclinatione Romani imperii', beginning: "Laetanti iam mihi et exultanti" (Decas III, Lib. I, ed. Basel, 1559, p. 393) and proceeds to Lib. X of this Decade. Then follow two books of a fourth Decade, of which the first is identical with the XIth book of Decas in in the Basel edition. The second is inedited: an extract relating to a mission to Abyssinia is printed by G. Williams (1.c. n, 227).
Lib. II: f. 22b, Lib. III: f. 426, Lib. IV: f. 60b, Lib. V (initial cut out) f. 76b, Lib. VI: f. 92, Lib. VII: f. 108b, Lib. VIII: f. 125, Lib. IX: f. 139, Lib. X: f. 156b. Ends f. 189. Each book has a fine initial on burnished gold (Lib. IX on silver): and the first lines of each are in Roman hand.

source_title: No. 90: Manuscripts and Printed Books from the Eighth to the Present Century
other_info:
Illuminated MS. on very thin vellum of the finest quality, 8vo. (175 by 110 mm.), 182 leaves, the last blank (I - XVII[8], XVIII[8], XIX[4]), written in Italy, probably Florence, about 1450-1460, in an exquisite humanistic hand, 23 lines to the full page, in black, red, blue and gold inks; there are 14 large illuminated initials of burnished gold, with white vine-leaf decorations against a blue, pale yellow, green and red background for the synopsis preceding each play and for the beginning of the plays, and, in two cases, also for the prologue; various lines and words in the beginnings in burnished gold letters, alternating with lines in blue and red ink; ca. 125 burnished gold initials at the beginning of every scene; the abbreviated names of the dramatis personae in red, blue, yellow and even gold in the text. Plain 18th or early 19th century brown russia binding. 
From the celebrated Vernon Collection, with Lord Vernon's bookplate in the front cover; sold at the Vernon sale, 1918, when it was acquired by Mr. Wilfred Merton. Merton MS. 31.

manuscript_binding: mar. rouge, doubl. encad. de fil. sur le dos et les plats, milieux de feuillages contenant un double C et un double A, ornés de quatre S barrés, tr. dor. (Rel. de Ève)
other_info: Ce manuscrit débute par une belle page ornée d'une miniature La Vierge allaitant l'enfant, contenue dans la lettre D (de Domine); de la lettre I (de Incipit) formée par une fleur qui se prolonge et orne la page entière; au base de la page deux anges soutiennent un écusson où sont peintes les armes de la famille de BAIGNY en Italie, écartelé en sautoir d'or et d'azur. Ensuite l'illustration continue par TRENTE-SIX SUPERBES miniatures de la plus grande beauté dont QUINZE à fond d'or, du plus bel effet, DOUZE à fond d'azur et NEUF en lettres historiées. Les miniatures à fond d'or sont: 1) La Vierge allaitant l'enfant. 2) Saint-Christophe portant l'enfant Jésus sur ses épaules à travers un torrent [...] Les miniatures à fond d'azur nous donnent les scènes suivantes: 1) La Nativité, curieuse miniature rarement traitée de la façon dont elle l'est ici: l'Enfant Jésus est tenu debout par deux femmes qui lui font prendre un bain dans un récipient avec pied. 2) L'Adoration des Mages [...] Ce précieux manuscrit a été exécuté dans l'Italie méridionale; cette origine est prouvée par la façon dont est représenté saint Nicolas de Myre, le caractéristique ici employé est souvent donné par les Italiens du Midi; par la présence au feuillet des armes d'une famille italienne; et aussi par les saint représentés dont beaucoup sont particuliers à l'Italie; nous remarquons Saint Dominique, dont l'ordre qu'il fonda se propagea rapidement en Italie; Saint Nicolas de Myre, très populaire en Italie; la ville de Bari passe pour posséder ses reliques [...] L'exécution des miniatures parait d'être de deux artistes différents, un ayant exécuté celles à fond d'or, l'autre celles à fond d'azur; quoique le dessin soit différent, l'ensemble est d'un goût parfait, le coloris est rendu avec la grâce digne du Giotto, surtout pour les miniatures à fond d'or. [...] L'illustration n'en a pas été terminée, un grand nombre de feuillets sont restés blancs au recto pour y apposer l'image du Saint dont l'oraison figure au verso du feuillet précédent [...] Trois miniatures sont en partie effacées.

other_info: The Florentine Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) undertook the project of translating and commentating on the corpus of Platonic and Neoplatonic works. He hoped that his contribution to the diffusion of these works would strengthen support for Plato’s replacing Aristotle as the philosopher of choice among Christians. The present manuscript contains a number of texts relating to this project. There are translations into Latin of a short work by Speusippus (who succeeded Plato as head of the Academy), of Alcinous’s De doctrina Platonis, and of the Aurea precepta (Golden verses) attributed to Pythagoras. These translations are dedicated to Ficino’s friend Giovanni Cavalcanti, to whom he also addresses a short letter on the subject of friendship and how best to use the teachings of Plato. Other miscellaneous texts follow, several of which are addressed to other contemporary Florentine figures.

other_info: Ff. 1 and 2 blank, 3b and 4a Table. In quires of 10, written in a bold Italian Gothic hand. bound at the end of the volume are some vellum leaves which formed the original fly-leaves and paste-downs at beginning and end of the original binding. On the leaf which lined the end board are a number of notes in a later hand, and also the date "M.cccxviii Fuit completus." This cannot refer to the MS itself, for if dated, the date would have been written formally by the scribe and not casually on the final end-leaf among some other notes. On the leaf which lined the first board is a short life of Valerius Maximus. References have been made to passages of Livy in a small neat hand in the margins throughout the volume. The calligraphy of this volume is of the style called bolognese, used in Italy in the 14th and part of the 15th centuries for important Classics.

(d'arezzo?) di soa mano gli anni di christo MCCCCXL". Vol. 2:  0.240 x 0.288; 89 ff. n. ch. Caractères de la même main du vol. précédent, mais plus petits; rubriques en rouge, à 2 cols. Au r. du 1, f.: Questo si e lo studio d atene ...molti gentiluomini e popolani fiorentini per rachonciallo e metterlo in asseto fatto per lo nobile uomo ditto... (?) e per suo maestro chiamo ser gigi chet uomo d'intelligenza [...] 4. f. v. explicit: volontier lo faro sanza mottegio. Suivent deux ff. blancs; 7. f. r.:  Orazione fecit mino di Vannnj sopra il pechatore (mannque à Bilancioni): Charissimo fratello io son la madre [...] Au r. de l'8. f. commence la Commedia: Inferno di dante alighieri: Nel mezzo dedl camin di nostra vita [...]. Au f.  27: Purgatorio di Dante Alighieri: Per chorrer miglior aqua alsa le vele [...] C. 44 r.: Paradiso di Dante alighieri: La gloria di cholui che tucto move [...]; f. 61 v., 1ère col. : L amor che move il cigio e l altre stelle/ Amen [...]; explicit f. 63 r.: Nel mezo del chamin di nostra vita / Amen. Dans la deuxième col. : Credo di Dante / Io scrissi gia d'amor piu volte rime; au v. : Dieci commandamenti di Dante: Dieci da dio abbiam commandamenti [...]; 64. f. r. : Incipit close Mini Vannis de Aretio super infernum dantis [...]. Au r. du f. 71: Questi sono e trionfi di messer francesco petrarcha / La notte che seghui l'orribil caso; f. 78 v.:  Or che fia dunque a rivederla in cielo; f. 79 r.: Al nome di dio e del buono inchominciare / [...] / queste parole sono tutte sentenzia / In veritade; explicit, f. 80 v.:  cholla santa vertu della speranza / Explicit deo gratias Amen; f. 81 r.: Questa sie una chanzona fatta per la figliuola d uno cittadino fiorentino e bono mercadante [...]; f. 87 v. explicit: Chosi fa chi ama la virtute / Finis.

other_info: Complete. The decoration consists of six splendidly illuminated double openings and seven pages with historiated initials. The style is that of Vante di Gabriello di Vante Attavanti, known as Attavante...and the manuscript was illuminated in his studio. The pairs of leaves forming the double openings have been removed from the volume and are preserved between sheets of glass. The double openings have on the left a large miniature and on the right a historiated initial with, above, an incipit in gold letters on a blue background and, below, two, three or four lines of text. Each page is framed with an elaborate renaissance border, with medallions containing heads or half-length figures set in panels of gold, red, blue and green and with putti and a variety of other ornament....The seven sections of the Office of the Virgin...begin with a large gold initial containing a bust of a female saint..there are also numerous gold initials on gold and coloured backgrounds and small gold initials on every page on backgrounds of blue, green or red.

other_info:
Illuminated MS. on fine vellum, executed in Florence towards the end of the 15th century, small 8vo. (127 by 80 mm.), 272 leaves (the first and the last two blank), 12 lines to a page, written in a superb humanistic hand; with 12 illuminated pages, arranged in pais facing each other, surrounded by magnificent borders, those on the left of the openings containing a full miniature, the pages on the right a miniature in an intial marking the beginning of the text; the borders have in the top panels the Sacred Initials supported by angels, etc., and in the lower and side panels the effigies of Apostles and Saints, surrounded by putti, birds, etc., within exuberant gold foliage; medallions of Roman Emperors etc., in the corners. Miniatures and borders are painted in liquid gold which is profusely applied, and glowing colours, predominantly royal and sky blue, purple, mauve, vermilion, green, yellow and sepia. 5 initials containing the heads of saints, with delicate floral borders extending the full length of the outer margins; some 200 finely ornamented smaller initials in gold and colours; Calendar (ff. 2-13) written in gold, blue and black; rubrics in gold and blue. 
Provenance: The position of the arms in the first opening suggests that the MS. belonged to a lady of the Giraldi family, married to a Guicciardini.

Written in small regular cursive miniscule in dark brown ink by a single scribe, headings in pale red, some sidenotes in red, initials in red; vertical ink catchwords. Stains on ff. 102, 109, few other spots of foxing and use, marginal wormhole on first few pages, but generally in VERY FRESH CONDITION with wide margins (though some sidenotes shaved). 17th-century(?) limp vellum, with title in brown ink on spine: 17th-century paper label on spine with library shelf mark.
other_info:
A MANUSCRIPT ON THE LIFE OF ST. JEROME, INDEPENDENT OF THE PRINTED VERSIONS, WITH A PERSONAL SELECTION OF HIS LETTERS, PROBABLY MADE BY OR FOR A WOMAN. The contents are as follows:
Folio 1: The epistle of St. Eusebius of Cremona (d. 423) to St. Damasus (d. 384) in Rome and to the Roman senator Theodore on the death of St. Jerome in Bethlehem.
Folio 33: Epistle of St. Augustine (d. 430) to St. Cyril (d. 387), bishop of Jerusalem, on the greatness of St. Jerome.
Folio 40: St. Cyril's reply to St. Augustine, with a detailed account of miracles performed by St. Jerome.
Folio 71: Epistle of St. Jerome to St. Paula, OTHERWISE UNRECORDED, in fifteen chapters on the Christian virtues.
Folio 86: Epistle of St. Jerome to St. Paula's daughter, St. Eustochia, in praise of virginity.
Our manuscript is independent of the printed editions; the Italian differs substantially from the printed translations, our manuscript does not include the list of miracles and testimonials present in the printed versions, and the chapter divisions differ in the first letter of St. Eusebius.
It is evident that the original owner was most interested in the two letters of Jerome to SS. Pauia and Eustachia since only these pages have annotations in the margins. As the subject matter of these epistles concerns women who have chosen the monastic life, it seems likely that this manuscript was either copied by or for a woman belonging to a religious order.

source_title: Brochure No. 14. Timeless Treasures: A Selection of Illuminated Manuscripts, Miniatures and Early Printed Books
manuscript_binding: 15th-century binding.
other_info: Incomplete. Border decoration, one illumination with bas-de-page. Final part of Common of Saints. First volume of an original set of three. 30 companion leaves in La Spezia (Museo Civico Amadeo Lia), Venice (Fondazione G. Cini), and some private collections. Four different illuminators worked on the three volumes, each with a distinct artistic background, but two of them embellished this codex: the first is like Maestro Daddesco and Pacino da Bonaguida, seen on ff. 242, and 253. The second artist, more progressive, illuminated ff. 254, 258, 303, and 315, featuring richly embroidered hems, set with precious jewels and clasps, pearls and gems, similar to the style of the Master of the Dominican Effigies.

Prickings usually visible in the fore-edge margin of quires I-II. Humanist script attributed to the Florentine notary set Giovanni di Piero da Stia (cf. de la Mare New Research I, 425-6, 499-500). Mersalo suggests this MS comes from the workshop of Vespasiano da Bisticci, but de la Mare does not include it in her list of Vespasiano manuscripts. Preface has a four-line white vine-stem initial M[ulta] with foliate ornament extending up and down the inner margin (2r); Books I-IV each with a three- to five-line initial in gold on a green and/or red ground framed in blue (4v, 32v, 66v, 96r) [see cat. pl. 14].

manuscript_binding: Sewn on five cords, with endbands; bound in early 19th-c. English (?) brown leather over pasteboards, with onlays of red leather dotted in gilt; spine in seven compartments without bands; marbled endpapers conjoint with pastedowns; gilt edges [cat. pl. 1]
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly MS. Lat. liturg. e. 28. i (paper) + 196 + ii (paper). Modern foliation in pencil i, 1-41a, 41b-197. 23 quires mostly of 10, but with numerous leaves missing. Ruled in pale grey-blue ink (quires I-VIII, XIV-XX) and pale brown (remainder). Headed in red; guides to rubrics and colored initials in tiny cursive script; capitals touched in pale yellow wash. | Contents. Hours of the Virgin, Use of Rome (imperfect); Long Hours of the Cross (misbound and imperfect); Penitential Psalms (imperfect); Litany and collects; Office of the Dead, Carmelite (?) use (imperfect); Calendar, very sparse. | Decoration. Four seven-line historiated initials, each below a colored panel with the heading of the text, mostly in square capitals of the humanist style, surrounded by a four-sided border containing further scenes in panels framed in gold. 1r Hours of the Virgin, initial D[omine]: Virgin and Child, lower border with two putti flanking a coat of arms. 81r Hours of the Cross, initial D[omine]: Man of Sorrows, standing in the tomb; 109r Penitential Psalms, initial D[omine]: King David playing the psaltery [cat. pl. 23]; 130r Office of the Dead, initial D[ilexi]: half-length skeleton holding scythe, border in a different style from others with lush acanthus foliage. Four-line painted foliate initials with burnished and painted gold at the start of each hour from Prime to Compline in the Hours of the Virgin; similar three-line initials in to the same hours in the Hours of the Cross; three-line initials in gold with blue, or blue with red, respectively, to Lauds of the Hours of the Virgin and the Cross; two-line initials to psalms, lessons, KL monograms in the calendar, etc.; one-line initials alternately in gold or blue to verses and other minor textual divisions. Illumination attributed by Garzelli to Mariano del Buono di Jacopo. | Made for a member of the Florentine Bellacci family (?): their (?) coat of arms on 1r, vert, a bend argent, with three uncertain five-pointed objects gules, the shield within a wreath held by two putti; matches the Bellacci arms if the five-pointed objects represent cinquefoils or roses. The responses of the nine lessons of the Office of the Dead are assigned by Ottosen to a wide variety of places, mostly French, but also to Sarum and Carmelite uses; the latter is assigned here on acccount of the Bellacci family's Carmelite links. Subsequent provenance includes Adolphe Labitte, Paris bookseller; perhaps bought by Thomas Buchanan with MS Buchanan e. 5 and Buchanan e. 136 in October 1857.

a plethora of exempla as well as plentiful quotes from scriptural, patristic, and lay authors. Known in only three manuscripts, only one of them complete, and unpublished, the collection merits a critical edition.

manuscript_binding: 19th-c. Parisian binding signed by (Alphonse?) Similer. Very dark green leather over pasteboards; covers tooled in gilt with outer frame enclosing another frame, center of each cover with four-pointed motif; doublures of brown leather; edges gilt
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] 144-5 x 99-102 mm (95-6 x 69-70 mm). iii (modern paper) + 484 + iii (modern paper). Pencil foliation ii-iii, 1-483 (marbled folios i and 484 not foliated). A previous modern pencil foliation on every tenth leaf was out of sequence after f. 330. 50 quires mostly of 10. Ruled in very faint grey or brown ink. Written in a "fere humanistica" bookhand, apparently by Dionisius de Castello, priest of S. Giovanni in Conca, Milan, throughout. | Contents. 1r-6v Ambrosian calendar, with an entry for almost every day of the year; each month headed by a verse on the unlucky days in brown ink. 7r-12v Roman calendar, with an entry for almost every day. 13r-192v Temporale. 193r-194v General Rubrics. 195r-v Table of scriptural readings for September. 195v-197r New Rubrics, in the order of the months. 197r-v Form of absolution from excommunication. 198v Rubric for feasts during the octave of Corpus Christi, here attr. Pope John XII. 199r blank. 199v-200r Hymn "Verbum caro factum est." 201r-277r Ferial Psalter. 277r-279r Litany. 279v Seven Penitential Psalms. 279v-280v Pater Noster, Ave Maria, Gloria in excelsis, Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Invitatory Psalm (Ps. 94) in two slightly different versions. 281r-291v Hymnal for proper and common feasts. 292r Prayers "Aue regina celorum," "Domine sancte pater omnipotens eterne deus," "Omnipotens sempiterne deus." 292r-v Miscellaneous notes: calendrical rubrics on finding dates; verses on the properties of fennel (also in 14th-c. Avignon, Bibliotheque du Musee Calvet MS 606). 293-425r Sancorale. 425v-431r Extra offices and prayers: Office of the Transfiguration, Office of Saint Anne, three short prayers of St. Anastasia. 432r-458r Common of Saints. 458r-460r Order of Grace. 460r-465r Office of the Virgin, Use of Rome. 465r-468v Office of the Dead, Use of Rome. 468v-476v Ritual of the Last Sacraments. 477r-478v Forms for blessing: salt and water, an altar, incense, bread. 478v-480v Additional lections for the Common of Saints. 480v Date 1465 and scribal colophon. 480v-481r Contemporary additional comemorations, by two of three different hands, of St. Thomas Aquinas, Sts. Hermagoras and Fortunatus, and the Holy Cross. | Decoration. Five historiated initials, of varying size, depicting mostly half-length figures. Seven similar smaller painted foliate initials. 4-, 3-, 2-, 1-line initials. | Signed and dated by Dionisius de Castello at end of volume; date "1464" also at end of Hymnal. Unidentified near-contemporary Italian owner(s) added Hermagoras and Fortunatas to the second calendar and the additions at the end of the volume, suggesting a special veneration (principal patrons at Udine, Gorizia, and Laibach (Llubljana)). Unidentified French Collector, 19th-c., with small gilt red leather bookplate, not that of Charles X of France as previously proposed. Collection of Baron Francois-Florentin-Achille Seilliere sold Sotheby's 24 February 1887 and four following days, lot 180, bought by Ridler for £13; probably bought by Buchanan immediately afterwards.

The structural outline includes very early instances of Arabic numerals.

Misc. 26, T. James 385. ff. 3+288, in fine minuscule hanging from lines ruled with a dry point. On f. iii.b (16th century): "Liber quondam Theodori Archiepiscopi Cantuar." And on f. 1a: "Hic liber scriptus per eum qui sc(ripsit) ypomnisticon grece." This latter note refers to the copy of the Hypomnesticon of Josippus in the [Cambridge] University Library, in the volume containing the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, etc. (CUL, Ms. Ff..1.24) which once belonged to [Robert] Grosseteste. In that is a note referring to the "paruum psalterium grecum." There is no doubt that this Psalter also belonged to Grosseteste: it is full of notes in his hand. I regard it as practically certain that it came from the Franciscan Convent at Oxford, to which Grosseteste bequeathed his books. For a connexion with Oxford is betrayed by the last page (f. 288b) on which is written [a provenance inscription of M. John Farley written in Greek]. John Farley was an official scribe of the University of Oxford. See on CCCC MS 423[.45] in which his name occurs.
The second last flyleaf is a printed leaf, cut at top and bottom, with alphabetical list of Latin 'incipits' of Psalms and then 'Numerus secundum Hebreos.' Printed at London by Richard Jugge and J. Cawood.
Cf. see James entry in his catalog for a detailed description of the Ms.'s contents, pp. 422-4 (Vol. II).

other_info:
2o fo: ecclesia. Fols. 373+ii (numbered fols. 374-5). Written in gothic textura semiquadrata, below top line; item 2 is written in textura semiquadrata, late 13th-century. 
Decoration: Fol. 4, at the opening of Genesis, has a full-page high I illustrating the works of the seven days, with gold leaf, above floral whirls at the foot, the text opening in gold leaf with blue and violet.
Fol. 3 has had a full-page illustration pasted on and then removed; only the bordering lines now remain. The single piece of illumination is ascribed to the early Oxford illuminator, William de Brailes. Nigel Morgan first made the identification, Early Gothic Manuscripts [I] 1190-1250 (London, 1982), 115, where he listed the MS among six previously unnoticed examples of de Brailes collaborating with other hands, apparently members of his workshop.
Cf. Christ Church, Oxford pdf-catalog entry.

titles: Leaves from a 13th-century Oxford Bible with early provenance in a Dominican house in Italy
places: Oxford, England, Great Britain, United Kingdom, Europe (England, Oxford)
manuscript_binding: not sequential, two columns of 43-44 lines numbered ‘3’ or ‘4’ at the bottom of the text block, ruled space: 110 x 65mm, ten illuminated initials in red, pink and blue with white penwork outlined in green to open: (i) II Corinthians (ii) prologue to Galatians; (iii) Galatians; (iv) prologue to Ephesians; (v) Ephesians; (vi) prologue to I Timothy; (vii) I Timothy; (viii) II Timothy; (ix) Philemon; and (x) Hebrews, (arranged as bifolia out of order on archival hinges, a couple of marginal tears).
other_info: Written and illuminated in Oxford around the middle of the 13th century: the leaves have numbering between the columns at every fifth line of text, an exclusively English feature deriving from Oxford, as described by M.A. and R.H. Rouse: ‘The purpose of the line-numbering was to enable the owner of a book to create his own index if he wished, or simply to be able to note down references to parts of books with precision. […] This reference system, still widely used today for classical texts and poetry, in the Middle Ages did not cross the Channel [...]’ (Authentic Witnesses, 1991, pp. 234-36). The removal of the Bible to Italy shortly after it was produced makes it an interesting witness to the 13th-century movement of books and students between Oxford and Italy, especially within the Dominican order. Sister leaves from this Bible can be identified on the basis of the unusual line-numbering, in which Arabic numerals are used with a more antique counting system (for a full account of this manuscript see: P. Kidd, ‘A Recently Dismembered Illuminated Bible, Probably from Oxford’, https://mssprovenance.blogspot.com/2020/03/a-recently-dismembered-illuminated.html).

other_info: The final two works, De judicio pulsuum and De urinis, are the work of Gilles de Corbeil [Aegidius Corboliensis], not Giles of Rome. Fol. 1-43v were the product of a copist who must have studied in Paris between 1286 and 1300, according to Laurence Moulinier-Brogi, “La Practica fratris du ms. Munich, Clm 267 : une lecture d’Avicenne par un religieux au xiiie siècle?” Archives d'histoire doctrinale et littéraire du Moyen Âge 84(2017) 157-312, at 177 : “...un petit codex de 53 folios daté d’entre 1286 et 1300 et mutilé en son début, qui doit sa relative notoriété au fait qu’il transmet une version du Thesaurus Pauperum de Petrus Hispanus. Outre ce célèbre texte, il renferme des textes anonymes : De virtute herbarum, De judicio pulsarum, De urinis, et la Concordantia Auctorum aux f. 25-42.” Moulinier-Brogi says (n. 94): “M. H. Rocha da Pereira a souligné que le copiste doit avoir au minimum étudié à Paris, puisqu’il complète la recette ‘De gutta rosacea’ par l’information suivante : ‘Hoc unguento usus fuit Magister Matheus et habuit ab Abbate qui dicebatur Potriaus, qui legit Cirurgiam super Pontem Parvum, Parisius’ (Obras de Maria Helena Rocha da Pereira, VI : Latin medieval, Fundaçao Calouste Gulbenkian, Imprensa da Universidade de oimbra 2014, p. 45, n. 1).” On fol. 54r, a (14th-century?) price, ‘xij s[solidi] par[isiensis]’.

source_title: "Préparations pharmaceutiques commandées par Louis XI", Bibliothèque de l'école des chartes, 55 (1894), pp. 721-722
titles: Incipiunt experimenta Bubikir Eirasis filii Zaccarie in doloribus juncturarum.; Practica puerorum (); Tractatus Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie in enarracione diversarum medicinarum expertarum a diversis actoribus medicine inventarum, qui intitulatur Experimentatio medicinalis.; Tractatus Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie de preparatione medicinarum, ut sine horribilitate saporis et odoris sumantur; Tractatus ejusdem qui nuncupatur liber presciencie Ypocratis, continens xxiii propositiones
authors: Rāzī, Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyā, 865?-925? (Razi)
other_info:
M. Claudin, libraire, nous a communiqué une copie de plusieurs traités du médecin Razi, faite à Paris en 1471, qui avait appartenu au xviiie siècle à Claude-Bernard Rousseau, auditeur des comptes, et plus
anciennement à « Monsieur de Massac, médecin à Orléans. » Le livre se termine par cette souscription :
« Explicit tractatus qui dicitur liber presciencie Ypocratis. Et in hoc
completur liber experimentorum Bubukir Eirasis filii Zaccarie, qui
completus fuit Parisius anno Domini millésimo quadringentesimo
septuagesimo primo, die vicesima mensis decembris. » Une assez curieuse particularité remarquée dans ce volume par M. Claudin, c'est la mention de la préparation de deux recettes qui fut
ordonnée par le roi Louis XI.
En marge de la page 108, en regard de ce passage : « Aliud mirabile
contra ventositatem fořtem, R/ : anisi cimini satureie..., » on lit ces mots : « 13a septembris, Rex precepit facere hic notatum. »
Un peu plus loin, sur la marge de la page 124, à côté du : « Capitulum secundum de medicinis ad ornatum faciei. Medicamen ad maculas magnas removendas et ad cutem subtiliendam et albificandam.
R/ : farine lupinorum partes quatuor..., » une main contemporaine de
la copie a tracé ces mots : « 13 septembris 1478, Rex precepit facere hic notatum. »
Ces deux notes peuvent être attribuées au médecin ou à l'apothicaire du roi Louis XI.

other_info: Schafer 1836, Part III, no. 590; Delisle 1905, 489-539; Morand 1961, 208, n. 16; Faye and Bond 1962, 334; Egbert (V.) 1974, 15-17, with figs.   Ina a long essay devoted to the manuscript, Leopold Delisle identified the owner, named as 'Blanche' several times in the text, as Blanche de France, Duchess of Orleans (1328-70).  It was Kathleen Mornad who first suggested in 1961 that Delisle's conclusion should be reconsidered because the style of the illustration of the Spencer volume parallelized that of such earlier Parisian manuscripts as the Life of St. Denis, presented to King Philip V (older brother of Charles IV) in 1317.  Virginia Wylie Egbert subsequently identified 'Blanche' as Blanche of Burgundy, in this way bringing into harmony the style of the illustration and the etxtual contents of the manuscript.

other_info: "This Book of Hours was produced in France, likely in Paris, around 1420. It contains a calendar, in French, with Parisian saints (fols. 1r-12v), followed by the Gospel Lessons (fols. 13r-16v), and the Obsecro te and O intemerata (fols. 17r-23r). The core of the book is composed of the Hours of the Virgin of the Use of Rome (fols. 25r-77v); the Penitential Psalms, Litany and Prayers (fols. 79r-94r); the Hours of the Cross (fols. 94v-97r); the Hours of the Holy Spirit (fols. 97v-100r); and the Office of the Dead (fols. 100v-129v). Each of these five major sections is introduced by a large miniature representing, respectively, the Annunciation (fol. 25r), Kind David in Prayer (fol. 79r), the Crucifixion (fol. 94v), Pentecost (fol. 97v), and a Burial Scene (fol. 100v). The first four of these miniatures have diapered backgrounds. The style of the miniatures is typical of Parisian illumination of the second and third decades of the fifteenth century. The style of the miniatures is reminiscent of the so-called Luçon Master."

titles: Hore beate Virginis Marie (Book of Hours)
manuscript_binding: mar. rouge, dent., double rangée de fil., doublé de mar. noir, comp. argentés, tr. dor. (Rel. anc.) [...] Le volume a été recouvert au XVIIe siècle d'une riche reliure et on a, à cette époque, ajouté en tête un feuillet de vélin sur lequel sont peintes les armoiries de Pierre de Guerchois, procureur général au Parlement de Rouen, mort en 1692.
other_info: Le volume débute par un calendrier en 12 feuillets; les noms des saints et des fêtes sont écrites en lettres d'or, en lettres rouges et en lettres bleues; ces noms sont écrits en français. Les diverses prières à la Vierge, les offices, les psaumes, etc., sont précédés de 6 ff. contenant le début des quatre Évangiles. Cette première partie du manuscrit se termine par diverses prières en français. Les 16 derniers feuillets contiennent diverses prières en l'honneur des saints. Ce manuscrit est richement décoré et enluminé. Toutes les pages du volume sont entourées de larges bordures avec arabesques formées de traits à la plume avec feuilles et fleurs en or, en rouge et en bleu. Ces bordures sont séparées de la marge latérale par un double filet, l'un d'or, l'autre blanc, bleu et rouge. Les bordures du calendrier sont ornées en outre de 24 petites miniatures de forme ronde représentant les signes du Zodiaque et les diverses occupations de chaque mois. Les miniatures sont au nombre de 43, dont 16 grandes et 27 de plus petite dimension. Les grandes miniatures représentent : Saint Jean dans l'île de Pathmos; la Salutation angélique; la Visitation; la Nativité; l'Annonciation aux bergers; l'Adoration des rois mages; la Circoncision; la Fuite en Égypte; le Couronnement de la Vierge; David en prières; la Crucifixion; la Pentecôte; l'Office des Morts; l'Enterrement; la Vierge et l'enfant Jésus; le Jugement dernier.  Les bordures de ces miniatures sont très riches et comprennent chacune 2 petites miniatures carrées dont le sujet se rapporte à celui de la grande miniature; c'est ainsi que dans la miniature représentant l'Adoration des rois mages on remarque les caxaliers et les chameliers apportant les présents; dans la bordure de la Fuite en Égypte figurent Hérode et le Massacre des Innocents, etc.    Attirons l'attention sur la peinture qui représente David et Bethsabée; contrairement à l'histoire biblique, la scène se passe dans une salle. Nous donnons la reproduction de cette page du manuscrit.   Les miniatures en tête de l'Office des Morts sont particulièrement intéressantes. Elles représentent, la première la Messe funèbre dans une église tendue de noir; le dais et l'autel sont recouverts de draperies d'azur semées de fleurs de lis d'or; les chapes des moines, les cierges, sont également garnis d'écus aux armes de France. La seconde nous montre l'enterrement dans une cimetière; au fond on aperçoit l'âme du défunt emportée au ciel par un ange qui éloigne le démon. Les miniatures de plus petite dimension représentent les Évangélistes, différents saints et saintes et plusieurs scènes de la vie du Christ. Toutes ces peintures sont l'œuvre d'artistes français et sont empreintes de la distinction qui caractérise les miniatures exécutées par les enlumineurs parisiens.

source_title: Books of Hours
places: Rouen, Normandy, France, Europe; Paris, France, Europe
manuscript_binding: Sewn on three bands and bound in 17th-century plain red-brown leather, incorporating a fragment of a 15th century manuscript [no further information].
other_info: Written in black ink in a formal gothic bookhand, "below top line"; rubrics in red, psalm titles usually in gold, canticle titles usually in red, the calendar in black, red, and blue. the text frequently strengthened, with some passages erased and re-written in the Middle Ages [sic].  Ten large historiated initials, six- to eleven lines high, each accompanied by a partial or full border of foliage and animals.  Probably illuminated in Paris, presumably for the woman depicted in the initial on fol. 188r, who doubtless lived in Rouen given the references to events there in the calendar.  The writing of the calendar must post-date 1247, when the feast of St. Eligius (1 December) was raised to a "triplex", and it must presumably also pre-date 1280, when the feast of St Ansbert (9 February) was similarly raised.  Stylistically the illumination can be dated to the 1260s.  14th-15th century additions suggest the manuscript was owned in the Bouches-du-Rhône region of southern France.

other_info: Superbe livre d'heures [...] dont la très belle ornementation est due à un des meilleurs artistes miniaturistes parisiens de cette époque. [...] d'une belle écriture gothique, et réglés avec soin, il a toutes ses pages, sans exception, illustrées par de gracieuses bordures où les rinceaux de feuillages, les animaux, les grotesques, les fleurs et les fruits, se combinent avec un goût parfait aux compartiments à fonds d'or, à fonds de couleur, de toutes nuances et de toutes formes. Soixante-treize miniatures traitées avec une grande délicatesse décorent ses principaux feuillets. Les vingt-quatre premières sont particulières au calendrier et représentent les douze signes du Zodiaque et les diverses occupations de chacun des mois de l'année. Parmi les quarante-neuf suivantes, quinze d'entre elles occupent la presque totalité d'u  feuillet, sont entièrement entourées par un encadrement à rinceaux et ont pour sujets les principales scènes du Nouveau Testament. Citons: S. Jean l'Évangéliste; la Visitation; le Baiser de Judo, l'Annonciation aux bergers, la Circoncision, le Couronnement de la Vierge, le roi David, Job sur son fumier et un charmant portrait de la Sainte Vierge. Le volume se termine par le propre de saints. Remarquons: S. Michel, S. Germain, S. Jean-Baptiste, S. Jacques, S. Christophe, S. Nicolas, Ste Geneviève, Ste Appoline, S. Eustache, Ste Agnès, etc., tous ces petits portraits sont très soignés dans leur composition. L'analyse du calendrier nous permet de penser que ce beau manuscrit a dû être exécuté à Paris; on y remarque en effet les principaux saints du diocèse: S. Marcel, S. Germain, Ste Geneviève cités trois fois, S. Eleuthère, S. Denis, S. Victor, S. Christophe, Ste Magdelaine, S. Landry, S. Étienne, etc. etc., -- Le 239e feuillet a été légèrement maculé. [PLATE]

other_info: Manuscripts of Aristotle are extremely rare on the market, especially ones with such impressive institutional provenance as the present copy. The Nicomachean Ethics is widely considered to be one of the most important of philosophical works: in it Aristotle outlines the theory of virtuous character based on the idea of finding a golden mean, along with valuable insights about friendship, courage, generosity and justice. Its influence in the European Middle Ages cannot be overstated, and one of the primary translations of the text was carried out - apparently at the request of Thomas Aquinas - by the Flemish Dominican William of Moerbeke, prolific translator of philosophical, medical and scientific texts. Moerbeke died in c.1286, and the colophon in the present manuscript describes the content as 'nove translationis'.

manuscript_binding: ii (paper) + 165 +ii (paper), ruled space: 88 x 58mm, rubrics in red, capitals touched in yellow, line-fillers and small illuminated initials throughout, each page with a panel border, ten large miniatures in arched compartments within full borders, erased inscriptions on ff.1, 73, 110, 117v and 165v (lacking 4 leaves, likely with miniatures, small spots of retouching to the first miniature and to the faces on ff.84 and one face on f.67v, some marginal staining, a few smudges and losses to the burnished gold, occasional marginal cropping). 18th-century calf gilt. other_info: The illumination has been attributed to the Master of Dreux Budé. A key figure in 15th-century Parisian painting, the Master was named from a dismembered Passion Triptych executed for Dreux Budé, a lawyer who rose high in the service of Charles VII. His evident debt to Netherlandish painting and his close stylistic relationship with the Coëtivy Master encouraged Reynaud to identify him with André d’Ypres, master in Tournai in 1428 who moved from Amiens to Paris in or after 1443 (see F. Avril and N. Reynaud, Les manuscrits à peintures en France 1449-1520, 1993, p.56); the Coëtivy Master was identified with André’s son, Colin d’Amiens, who also settled in Paris. The subsequent discovery that André d’Ypres died in July 1450 in Mons after returning from a pilgrimage to Rome is consonant with the Master’s evident connection with van der Weyden, also in Rome that year, but has entailed a re-evaluation of an oeuvre usually considered to extend well into the 1450s (D. Vanwijnsberghe, ‘Du nouveau sur le peintre André d’Ypres, artiste du Nord installé à Paris’, Bulletin monumental, 158 (2000), pp.365-369; D. Thiébaut et al., Primitifs francais découvertes et redécouvertes, 2004, pp.92-101).

A finely illuminated Book of Hours from the circle of the Master of Anne of Brittany that maintained its function as a family chronicle through twelve generations and four centuries.  
The book is for the Use of Langres, with saints specially revered there in the Calendar - John Abbot of Réome (28 Jan.), Didier, Bishop of Langres (23 May), Winebald (29 May), Mammas (17 August), dedication of the church of St Mammas, the Cathedral of Langres, (26 August), translation of Mammas (10 Oct.) – and the Litany – Benignus, Didier, Mammas, Gengulphus, Lupus and Clarus. Its decoration, however, shows that it was made in Paris.

manuscript_binding: i + 90 leaves, the final gathering a later addition, written space 120 x 70mm, rubrics in red, line-endings and one-and two-line initials in liquid gold on grounds of red, blue or maroon, larger initials in liquid gold or blue on maroon or red grounds decorated with liquid gold, a three-sided border on every text page and most blanks with devices, mottoes, symbols, grotesques, secular figures, saints and angels on grounds finished with liquid gold, 24 small Calendar miniatures, four small miniatures, thirteen full-page miniatures in full borders and, in the later addition, four large miniatures above large initials in blue with red grounds and infills of flower or fruit sprays on gold within full borders. other_info: The text is for the use of Amiens and its calendar has in red Sts Firmin (8 January and 1 and 25 September), Honoré (16 May) and Fuscian and Gentian (7 December); the litany includes Fuscian; Salvius is among the memorials. Its exceptional borders relate it to a small group of Hours of Amiens use, suggesting that the manuscript was mostly illuminated there; the French orthography indicates a Picard scribe. It was then probably sent to Paris for its miniatures - stylistically the first two relate to Rouen and the remainder to Paris, a combination more likely in Paris. There are numerous irregularly placed devices, some on blue shields, that might indicate ownership: the initials JG BL GY GM BJ GR; the St Andrew’s Cross and firesteels of the Dukes of Burgundy, as used by their Habsburg successors; the mottoes: JE ME PLAINS, AVE MARIA, GLORIA, AMOR; blue shields with sunbursts or silver ?stars between gold ?clouds, in varying numbers, and an illegible design in tarnished silver seem unlikely to be armorial bearings, although the sunburst and the illegible design reappear below the later miniatures on ff.88v and 89v. Below the two added miniatures with men praying, ff.86 and 87v, appears a shield gules, three keys or in fess, within an orle of chain or. One of these miniatures is St James, so the patron was perhaps named Jacques, which would fit with the JG and Y border initials. There are several 16th- and 17th-century inscriptions, some faint and some deliberately obscured, all relating to Normandy or families of Norman origin.

source_title: Catalogue de manuscrits avec miniatures des XIIIe au XVIIIe siècles
manuscript_binding: velours cramoisi,  tr. dor.
other_info: Il est orné de cinquante-neuf miniatures, de trente-six grandes lettres majuscules en couleur, avec ornements sur fond d'or, et de plus de milles lettres initiales moyennes et petites en or sur fond de couleur, disséminées dans le volume. Les pages contenant les miniatures et les grandes majuscules sont décorées d'un bel encadrement consistant en arabesques auxquels sont associés des perroquets, des paons et une grande variété d'oiseaux, des bustes d'hommes et de femmes émergeant de calices, de nombreux grotesques, d'anges chantant ou jouant de divers instruments, etc. En outre, les pages, au nombre de 300 environ, où figurent les initiales moyennes, ont un listel bordant la partie extérieure du texte duquel partent des branchages rehaussés de fleurettes en or et couvrant les marges sur trois côtés. Toutes ces peintures sont bien exécutées et d'une bonne conservation. Le volume s'ouvre par une miniature placée au v[erso] du premier f.  et représentant un écusson où sont peintes les armoiries de son premier possesseur: D'or, à la croix pattée de gueules cantonnée, au 1 et 4 d'une fleur de lis d'azur, au 2 et 3 d'une rose au naturel; écartelé d'argent plein. L'écu soutenu par deux lions d'or est surmonté d'un casque d'argent ayant pour cimier une aigle éployée de sable. Le tout est renfermé dans un cadre composé de fleurs sur fond or. Les autres miniatures se divisent en 37 grandes et 21 petites, ces dernières représentant des saints et des saintes. Les grandes, cintrées dans   le haut, et mesurant de 60 à 68 mill. de hauteur et environ 40 mill. de largeur, sont toutes placées aux versos des pages avec les rectos blancs. Nous en signalerons quelques-unes qui sortent un peu des sujets ordinairement représentés dans les livres d'Heures: Saint Louis, évêque de Toulouse, couvert d'un grand manteau bleu fleurdelisé. - Saint François d'Assises, agenouillé au pied de la croix, reçoit les stigmates qui partent des plaies de Notre-Seigneur et viennent s'incruster sur ses membres. - Moïse, entouré du peuple prosterné, reçoit des mains de Dieu les Tables de la loi. - La Mort, avec des ailes rouges, à cheval, décoche des flèches sur un groupe d'hommes et de femmes où tous les rangs de la société sont représentes; deux personnes gisent à terre. - Les Destinataires du volume, un homme et une femmes, sont agenouillés dans les champs et prient, les yeux tournés ver le Ciel où l'on voit le Père éternel, Jésus-Christ, la sainte Vierge et plusieurs saints entourés de rayons de gloire. - Un chœur d'anges dans une église. - Le Saint-Sacrement porté par un moine vêtu d'une robe blanche et d'un grand manteau bleu. - Les Destinataires cités co-dessus spot agenouillés dans une église; en face d'eux sont également agenouillés un homme et une femme plus âgés. - Sainte Hélène découvre la croix de Notre-Seigneur. L'impératrice, couronne en tête, vêtue d'un grand manteau bleu frangé d'or, regarde deux ouvriers qui creusent la terre; auprès d'elles se tiennent deux seigneurs. Quelques-uns de ces sujets et plusieurs de ceux des miniatures traditionnelles qui ornent ce manuscrit sont placés dans ce gracieux paysages avec des villes dans le lointain.

authors: Augustine of Hippo, Saint, 354-430 (Augustine, of Hippo, Saint, 354-430); Raoul, de Presles, 1316-1382 (Raoul de Presles) [Tr]
artists: Maître d'Orose (Orosius Master and his workshop) [Workshop]
manuscript_binding: Scottish brown Russia leather binding by James Scott of Edinburgh, gilt boards and spine, circa 1790; spine title, Augustin De la cite de Dieu M.S.
other_info: "This manuscript is a deluxe illuminated copy of the first five books of Raoul de Presles's French translation of and commentary on Augustine's City of God, a theological and historical treatise countering the claim that the Roman Empire fell because of its conversion to Christianity. The French translation, commissioned by Charles V, was completed in 1375, and this copy of the first five books of the text was illuminated by the Orosius Master and his workshop in Paris, circa 1408-1410, possibly for Jean, duc de Berry. The first column miniature in the manuscript, marking the dedication to Charles V, depicts Raoul de Presles presenting his translation to the king (fol. 1r). A three-quarter-page miniature of the City of God and the City of the Pagans marks the beginning of the first book (fol. 5r) and double-column miniatures mark the beginning of each of the following books, as is true for many illuminated copies of this text. In addition, however, the first and second books of this manuscript are extensively illuminated with column miniatures at the beginning of each chapter, often drawing on the commentary for historical and literary source material. The text is written in two columns of textualis semi-quadrata script. At least one leaf is missing at the end of the volume, where the text breaks off near the end of the fifth book."

places: France, Europe (France, likely Paris?); Paris, France, Europe (France, likely Paris?)
other_info:
UNIQUE TEXT COMPILED FROM TWO PRINTED EDITIONS. This manuscript was copied in the circle of the eminent humanists who founded the Sorbonne Press in Paris, Jean Heynlin and Guillaume Fichet. It is based on two editions of Cicero’s De officiis, one printed in Paris in 1471-1472 by the
Sorbonne Press, the other printed first in Venice in 1481, of the first edition of Pietro Marso’s influential commentary. The humanist scribe (Heynlin?) of the present manuscript was clearly a careful reader of both imprints, and it seems
likely that this codex was a preparatory manuscript for another edition of Cicero by the Sorbonne Press.

other_info: This small and intimate volume of courtly love poetry was almost certainly made for a member of the French royal court in the time of King Louis XII and Anne of Brittany. Collections such as this are not common (only three similar manuscripts have sold in the last century).

places: Northern France, France, Europe (Northern France (Paris?)); Paris, France, Europe (Northern France (Paris?))
other_info: This is among the smallest examples known of the Paris “pocket” Bible. One tiny volume contains the entire biblical text, copied in a minute script on tissue-thin parchment and adorned with small painted initials, including five that are historiated. Its text belongs to the recension known as the Paris Bible, the direct ancestor of the sixteenth-century Clementine Vulgate. Although not in pristine condition, this is nonetheless an excellent example of a type of Bible of great importance both to the history of the Vulgate and to the history of the book in the Middle Ages.
