other_info: fos. 238 + vi. With Parisian Calendar, added mid 13th cent. With additions of late 13th and early 14th centuries. The book was extensively repaired at the edges throughout in the early 14th century, and from the care and skill devoted to the repairs must have been a highly-valued possession. Decorative initials in red and blue pen-work and large initials in gold and colours of early 13th, late 13th and early 14th centuries. Miniature of the Crucifixion with seven saints, and one historiated initial of priest celebrating Mass, both with bar borders and ivy leaf decoration, added c. 1340, at the Canon of the Mass. A detailed account of the provenance and composition of the book is written by S.C. Cockerell on the first fly leaf. He acquired it in 1922 in two separate portions, A, of 186 leaves, and B, of 52 leaves. Exhibited at the Royal Academy, French Art, 1932, no. 751d., and in Paris, Palais National des Arts, 1937, Chefs-d'oeuvre de l'Art Francais, no. 746.

other_info:
The Lyghfield Bible
late 13th century
A pocket Bible probably produced in Northern France, probably Paris. 

With prologues of Jerome and Interpretation of Hebrew names, with 66 decorated initials, 72 historiated initials, 10 very large historiated initials and one full-page Genesis initial with seven scenes of the Life of Christ. 

With inscription identifying it as the Bible of Master Thomas Trussel, who is likely to be the man of that name who was appointed Archdeacon of Middlesex in 1331 but did not take up the office. 
Also faded inscription identifying it as the Bible of 'Dominus' William Lyghfield (Lighfyld'), a monk of Canterbury Christ Church. 
Lyghfield was one of the monks who received a pension at the Reformation, becoming a minor canon. 
A further faded inscription (legible only with UV light) almost certainly reads 'Christ Church Canterbury' in Latin. 

Purchased at auction at Bloomsbury Book Auctions in July 2018 from the Schoyen Collection with support from the National Heritage Memorial Fund, the Friends of Canterbury Cathedral, the Friends of the National Libraries and a private donation. 
Described in the auction catalogue as 'The Canterbury Trussel Bible' and identified one leaf as being missing.

other_info:
(Size refers to text area only - see below):
"Illuminierte lateinische Pergamenthandschrift, Nord Frankreich, wahrscheinlich Paris, ca. 1440. 119 Blätter, 17 Zeilen pro Seite, braune Tinte, gotische Schrift, Schriftspiegel 95 x 64 mm, zahlreiche 2 - und 3-zeilige Initialen in Gold, Pink, Blau und Weiß; 17 drei Viertel Bordüren mit Blattranken in polychrome und Gold und fünf Miniaturen in Goldumrahmung..."
"Tls. berieb. u. schmutzfl. Loch b. der gr. Initiale unter der ersten Miniatur, tls. Randläsuren. - Die Miniaturen enthalten: die Verkündigung (f.13r), König David knieend neben seiner Harfe (f.21r), das Grab des Lazarus ( f.32v), die Kreuzigung (f.116r) und die Arma Christi (f.118v). - BOOK OF HOURS. Illuminated Latin manuscript on vellum. Northern French, likely Paris, c.1440. 119 leaves, 17 lines per page, brown ink, gothic bookhand, written space 95 x 64 mm, numerous 2- and 3-line initials in gold, pink, blue and white; 17 three-quarters borders of leafy tendrils in polychrome and gold; and FIVE ARCH-TOPPED MINIATURES in burnished gold frames. 19th century vellum. Some rubbing and soiling, hole to large initial under first miniature, occasional cropping to borders, binding defective. The miniatures comprise: the Annunciation (f.13r), King David kneeling beside his harp (f.21r), the tomb of Lazarus (f.32v), the Crucifixion (f.116r), and the Arma Christi (f.118v)." (from www.kiefer.de)
This record identified with thanks to Max Schmitz.

source_title: Medieval manuscripts from the collection of T.R. Buchanan in the Bodleian Library, Oxford [Bodleian Library, University of Oxford, 2001 (Peter Kidd)]
titles: Books of Hours, Use of Paris, in Latin and French
manuscript_binding: Sewn on three cords; green and brown end bands; bound in French 19th-c. dark brown or black leather over pasteboards, with contemporary pastedowns; spine with five false raised bands; gilt edges; boxed 1994
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly Bodleian MS Lat. liturg. e. 23. ii+174+ii (endpapers front and back are modern parchment bifolia). 162-3 x 104-6 mm. (88-9 x 52-7 mm.). Quires of 8. Fine regular gothic book hand. Ruled in pale brown ink, with single vertical bounding lines extending the full height of the page. Calendar with 16 ruled lines per page [i.e. 15 written lines]. Script is smaller and markedly more angular from the start of the Office of the Dead (104r), but perhaps all by a single scribe. Shade of ink changes from quire to quire. Headings in red; marginal guides to the rubricator occasionally visible. Modern foliation, in pencil i-ii, 1-68a, 68b-175. | Contents include Calendar in French (type for Paris Books of Hours); Gosepl Pericope from John; Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris, with three lessons at Matins; Hours of the Cross; Hours of the Holy Spirit; Penitential Psalms; Litany and collects ("Deus cui proprium est miserere semper et parcere" and "Fidelium deus omnium conditor et et redemptor"; Office of the Dead (Romanized Paris Use?); Prayers to the Virgin and to the Trinity in Latin and French ("O intemerata...orbis terrarum" (feminine forms), "Obsecro te..." (masculine forms), "Ave Maria gracia plena dominus tecum. Martir cum martiribus transgladiata...," "E tres certaine esperance...," "O sancta trinitas atque indiuisa vnitas uera...") [see cat. for descriptions and notes on contents]. | Decoration comprises 14 miniatures, most above four lines of text; figures with grisaille draperies, some in a rudimentary landscape with a ground line and trees, set against a diaper or patterned background; in a rectangular frame with gold bosses at the corners; above a three- or four-line initial, from which sprout ivy-leaf decoration surrounding the text and image on all four sides; sewing-holes on the outer margin of the first few miniatures, presumably from protective textile veils. 13r Pericope: St. John the Baptist holding Agnus Dei. 15r Hours of the Virgin, Matins: Annunciation. 27v Lauds: Visitation. 40r Prime: Nativity. 46v Terce: Annunciation to the Shepherds. 51r Sext: Adoration of the Magi. 55v None: Presentation in the Temple. 60v Vespers: Flight into Egypt. 68r Compline: Coronation of the Virgin. 73v Hours of the Cross: Crucifixion. 78r Hours of the Holy Spirit: Pentecost. 83v Penitential Psalms: God seated, turning away from the Tablets of the Old Law to bless covered chalice and wafer [cat. pl. 15]. 104r Office of the Dead: funeral service, with black-clad mourners, and clerics singing, on which an open book is inscribed in minute script with the Introit of the Mass of the Dead; 156r O intemerata: Virgin and Child enthroned, a laywoman in prayer before them [cat. pl. 16]. Pacht & Alexander relate the style to BnF MSS Fr. 22912-3, Augustine (Raoul de Presles) Cite de Dieu, 1376-80. | MS presumably made in Paris for the laywoman depicted on 156r (the prayer starting on this page uses feminine forms). Subsequently owned by an unidentified German prince-archbishop, whose armorial bookplate was transferred from previous binding to the present pastedown [cat. pl. 17]. Subsequent provenance includes an unidentified French owner and an unidentified French bookseller, before the acquisition by Messrs. T. & W. Boone.

source_title: Medieval manuscripts from the collection of T.R. Buchanan in the Bodleian Library, Oxford [Bodleian Library, University of Oxford, 2001 (Peter Kidd)]
titles: Books of Hours, Use of Paris, in Latin and French
manuscript_binding: Modern sewing probably on five cords, without endbands; recased in a 16th/17th-c. French limp parchment over parchment 'boards'; the covers tooled in gilt with foliate and interlace designs within framing lines; spine with 4(originally 6) sewing supports
other_info:
[See cat. for additional notes, description, and bibliography.] Formerly MS. Lat. liturg. e. 29. 134-6 x 94-7 mm (c. 77 x 47 mm). Modern pencil foliation i-ii, 1-154. 23 quires mostly of 8. Ruled in pale red ink (19 ruled lines, i.e. 18 written lines, except 17 ruled lines in quire XIX). The added leaves (1-3, 152) ruled with 19-21 lines in pale leadpoint. Lettre batarde in two different sizes of script, according to liturgical function. At least three main scribes, responsible for 16r-125v, 126r-133v (quire XIX, with different ruling), and the added leaves (1-3, 151-2) in a much later rounded humanist hand, perhaps imitating books printed in Roman type. Unclear whether the calendar may be by another scribe. | Contents. 1r-3v (quire I) Hymns added 16th/17th c. ("Veni sancte spiritus," "Veni creator spiritus," "Vexila regis prodeunt," "Veni redemtor gentium"). 4r-15v (quires II-III) Calendar, in French. 16r-21v Gospel Pericopes. 21v-25r "Oratio ad beatam mariam. Obsecro te..." 26r-71v Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris. 72r "[Omnipotents sempiterne deus...]" starting imperfect at the fifth word due to the loss of a leaf after fol. 71. 73r-76v Hours of the Cross. 77r-80r Hours of the Holy Spirit (title on 76v). 80v ruled but blank. 81r-91v Seven Penitential Psalms. 91v-96r Litany and collects. 97r-136v Office of the Dead, Use of Paris, starting imperfect. 136v-137v Decotion, with heading in French "Pour les trespassez." 138r-150r Suffrages and other prayers. 151r-152v Hymns added 16th/17th c. ("Christe redemptor omnium ex patre patris...," "Christe qui lux es et dies..."). | Decoration. Four large miniatures with arched tops, above 3, 4, or 5 lines of text. 26r Hours of the Virgin, Matins: Annunciation. 73r Hours of the Cross: Crucifixion. 77r Hours of the Holy Spirit: Pentecost, Apostles and Virgin [cat. pl. 26]. 138r Suffrage to the Trinity: The Trinity. 25 (of an original 26?) small miniatures, framed in liquid gold on the upper three sides, 6-9 lines high (saints and devotional scenes). 24 small miniatures illustrating the Occupations of the Months and Zodiac signs, mostly set in landscapes, in the lower margin of the calendar. Four-sided borders to pages with miniatures, two-sided borders in the calendar, one-sided borders in the fore-edge margin of pages with a two-or three-line initial. Two- or three-line initials in red, blue, and white, with painted gold decoration, at the start of sections; one-line initials for verses and minor textual divisions. By two main artists: the larger miniatures by an artist in a late gothic style, while the calendar and suffrages are by an artist in an essentially renaissance style. The borders of the calendar (consistent with rest of volume) appear to have been executed before the calendar miniatures [see cat. pl. 25]. | 16th/17th-c. additions probably added at the time of the present binding by an unidentified French (?) owner.

The contemporary addition on 161v-162v (Suffrage to St. Barbara) is in a finer 15th-c. gothic bookhand, but in lesser-quality ink. | Contents. 1r-12v (quire I) Calendar, in French. 13r-17r Gospel Pericopes. 17r=25v Prayers to the Virgin ("Obsecro te," "O intemerata," "Salue mater dolorosa / Iuxta crucem lacrimosa"). 26r-75r Hours of the Virgin, unidentified use. 75v added texts relating to Sens (response and versicle and a suffrage to Saints Sabinianus and Potentianus of Sens). 76r-87v Penitential Psalms. 88r-94r (rubric on 87v) Litany and collects. 94v-101r (rubric on 94r) Hours of the Cross. 101v-107v (rubric on 101r) Hours of the Holy Spirit. 108r-113r Fifteen Joys of the Virgin, in French. 113v-116r (rubric on 113r The Seven Requests of Our Lord, in French. 116r-v Prayer to the Holy Cross, in French rhyming verse ("Saint uraie crois aouree / Qui du corps dieu fus a ornee"). 116v=118v Devotion to the Passion of Christ (John and Matthew). 118v-119v Verses of St. Bernard. 120r-161r Office of the Dead, use unidentified. 161v-162v added suffrage to St. Barbara. 163r-188r Suffrages, an unusually long series. | Decoration. 12 of an original at least 15 large fine miniatures, all but three above 4 lines of text; most with ogee-curved tops, though many cropped at top; one trefoil-shaped (94v) and one rounded (101v). Each with a three-sided frame usually of gold and painted foliage. Most damaged causing underdrawing to be visible in some plates. Miniatures in the style of the Master of the Rohan Hours (this MS is not mentioned in Meiss and Thomas). 13r Pericopes: St. John on Patmos. 26r Hours of the Virgin, Matins: Annunciation. 37v Lauds: Visitation. 53v Terce: Annunciation to shepherds. 63v Vespers: Flight into Egypt. 70r Compline: Coronation of the Virgin. 76r Penitential Psalms: David in Penitence. 94v Hours of the Cross: Crucifixion. 101v Hours of the Holy Spirit: Pentecost. 108r Fifteen Joys: Virgin nursing Child. 113v Seven Requests: The Last Judgement. 120r Office of the Dead: Funeral service. Vertical borders to every page, both sides of text, with sylized and semi-naturalistic plants. | Presumably made for the unidentified laywoman depicted on 108r. The unidentified use does not correspond with Troyes, Angers, or Paris, three uses for which the Rohan Master produced Books of Hours. Saints in the litany point towards the St.-Omer / St.-Bertin region. Subsequent provenance includes a near-contemporary owner, diocese of Sens. Symeon de Roussel, 1694, possibly responsible for present binding, inscribed on 188v [see cat.]. 19th-c. French owner inscribed "Les 7. alegresses de la Ste Vierge" 107v.

Lettre batarde throughout. 15th century inscription on f. 200v, "Ce livre appartient a..." is partly erased, thus the early provenance remains unknown. manuscript_binding: French humanistic script, brown ink, red rubrics, paragraph marks in gold, 2- to 4-line initials throughout in red and blue. 19th-century binding.
other_info: Tardif (c. 1440–c. 1500) was one of the foremost French humanists of the fifteenth century. His Basis grammaticae, of which this is the autograph, was written for his young pupil Charles Mariette, godson of Louis XI’s brother Charles de Guyenne. The text is a basic introduction to Latin grammar divided into eight parts, which consider nouns, pronouns, verbs, participles, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections. It also includes conjugation tables for four verbs, with some glosses in French for the verb amare (to love). The second half of the manuscript contains a commentary, in which Tardif explains his purpose – to give an account of Latin grammar “purged of the vices of the Barbarians”. This is the first French humanist grammar; it was printed in the early 1470s.

source_title: No. 90: Manuscripts and Printed Books from the Eighth to the Present Century
titles: Bible, in Latin. - Isaiah to Colossians, with the Prologues of St. Jerome
manuscript_binding: Binding of wooden boards in medieval style, broad back covered with pigskin and blind-tooled.
other_info:
Large folio (455 by 305 mm.), 177 leaves, signatures I-XVIII in tens (I [1-3] missing, text incomplete at end) 2 columns, headline (in red) and 40-41 lines to a page, written in a fine large Gothic hand. With 2 large miniatures of superlative quality representing St. Luke and the Decapitation of St. Paul, executed in burnished gold and colours, both within an initial P; 40 large ornamental initials in blue and red or in various colours; numerous smaller blue and red pen initials; beginnings and endings of the various books written in red. Ruling with plummet. 
A monument of French 13th century illuminating during the reign of St. Louis which produced one of the greatest works of medieval art, the Bible Moralisee, and, connected with it, a small group of other illuminated MSS., mainly executed for the Royal circle. It is to that celebrated Bible and one or two MSS. of the same group to which our MS. appears to be closely related. As Comte A. de Laborde has pointed out (La Bible Moralisee, V, pp. 170 et seq.), the group cannot be ascribed to a single hand or one atelier, but resemble each other in style and technique. The style of our MS. calls to mind especially the New Testament pictures in the Toledo MS. of the Bible Moralisee (op. cit. IV, plate 638 et seq.) and the Psalter of Queen Ingeborg at Chantilly (cf. J. Meurgey, Les Principaux MSS. du Musee Conde, pl. X-XIII) in which also the facial types have much in common with SS. Luke and Paul in our miniatures; the figure of the executioner in our Execution of St. Paul may also be compared to that of David on fol. 37v in the Psalter of Queen Ingeborg. Pierpont Morgan MS. 74, a Book of Hours, is another book with which our MS. shows unmistakable affinities. (cf. Burlington Fine Arts Club Catalogue, 1908, pl. 83).
provenance: Merton, Wilfred, 1888-1957; Martin Breslauer (firm)

source_title: No. 90: Manuscripts and Printed Books from the Eighth to the Present Century
titles: Book of Hours - Hours of the Virgin, Use of Paris
manuscript_binding: In an old velvet binding
other_info:
Illuminated MS. on vellum, executed in France, probably Paris, in the early part of the 15th century; 315 leaves (ff. 31 and 136 blank), 16mo. (92 by 65 mm., area of the written page c. 66 by 37 mm.), 13 lines, written in a good small Gothic hand, Calendar and some passages written in black and red. With 25 half-page miniatures (c. 47 by 33 mm.), surrounded by full-page borders with characteristic ivy-leaf decorations, and 1 miniature within an initial O. With 257 decorative initials with foliage ornamentations against a background of burnished gold, with ivy-leaf and flower borders, heightened with gold, extending to half, and often to the full length of the margins. Several thousand smaller gilt initials and line-endings, heightened with gold. 
A minuscule early 15th century Book of Hours of great charm and artistic interest; many of its miniatures show such unmistakeable affinities with the work of the celebrated Master of the Hours of the Marechal de Boucicaut and his atelier, that it must be assumed that they were painted by an artist who belonged to that workshop.

Illuminated MS. on vellum, executed in France, probably Paris, C. 1470. 205 leaves (should be 206), 4to. (215 by 148 mm.), 15 lines to a page, written in a bold Gothic hand, some words in red, the Calendar in gold, blue and red; ruled in pale red. With 31 outstanding miniatures, 10 of these (c. 100 by 70 mm.) on full pages, surrounded by borders of flowers, foliage, animals and grotesques, and 22 smaller miniatures (between 50-60 by 45-50 mm.) all painted in colours both brilliant and delicately shaded, principally blue, azure, vermilion, orange, pink, mauve, green, golden-brown, yellow and white, with matt gold profusely applied; the borders richly heightened with burnished gold; decorated with c. 170 large blue initials heightened with white and filled with foliage in blue, orange and white, with backgrounds of burnished gold; many smaller gold initials against purple and light blue backgrounds, heightened with white, line-endings of purple and blue compartments heightened with burnished gold and white. 
In a magnificent French Renaissance binding of light brown calf, profusely gilt and heightened with silver; on sides a border of azured ovals enamelled with silver; large gilt centre-piece composed of strap work and arabesques painted silver, surrounded by a seme of diamond-shaped small tools, large azured and dotted arabesque corner-pieces heightened with silver; 5 raised bands on back, at head and tail a line of azured ovals, the other compartments filled with arabesques; gilt and gauffred edges.

It is thus described by a French expert: "Ravissant manuscript [sic.], parfaitment conservee, sur velin de 214 feuillets, ecrit en France (Paris ?) au fin du XV Siecle. Le volume est ornee de 18 superbe miniatures de la grandeur de la page comprises dans de riches bordures avec arabesques de feuillages, fleurs, fruits, oiseaux, etc. L'on y trouve feuillets 21 a 24, une oraison a la Vierge en vers francais. "Ah glorieuse Pucelle, Je te salue comme telle ... ... " a la suite, une autre oraison egalement en francais. Voici le sujet des miniatures: L'Annonciation, La Nativite de N.-S., L'Annonciation aux Bergers, L'Adoration des Mages, La Presentation au Temple, La Fuite en Egypte, La Purification, La Vierge en prieres, Saint Joseph et Sainte Anne, La Naissance du Christ, Jesus-Christ et les apotres, Le prophete David, La Descente du Saint-Esprit, Jesus crucifie, La Messe des morts, La Mise au tombeau, Trahison de Judas. Il est orne d'un grand nombre de lettres initiales en or et en couleur; au recto de toutes les pages, se trouve une large bande egalement ornementee. Toutes les miniatures sont encadrees d'ornements en or et en couleurs representant des fleurs, des oiseaux, des insectes, des animaux et figures fantastiques, ainsi que des personnages en costume du XVe siecle. Dans l'ornementation de 6 de ces miniatures l'on voit au bas les armoiries de la famille Seguier. Tres beau manuscrit d'une grande fraicheur."

titles: Leaves from a 13th-century Oxford Bible with early provenance in a Dominican house in Italy
places: Oxford, England, Great Britain, United Kingdom, Europe (England, Oxford)
manuscript_binding: not sequential, two columns of 43-44 lines numbered ‘3’ or ‘4’ at the bottom of the text block, ruled space: 110 x 65mm, ten illuminated initials in red, pink and blue with white penwork outlined in green to open: (i) II Corinthians (ii) prologue to Galatians; (iii) Galatians; (iv) prologue to Ephesians; (v) Ephesians; (vi) prologue to I Timothy; (vii) I Timothy; (viii) II Timothy; (ix) Philemon; and (x) Hebrews, (arranged as bifolia out of order on archival hinges, a couple of marginal tears).
other_info: Written and illuminated in Oxford around the middle of the 13th century: the leaves have numbering between the columns at every fifth line of text, an exclusively English feature deriving from Oxford, as described by M.A. and R.H. Rouse: ‘The purpose of the line-numbering was to enable the owner of a book to create his own index if he wished, or simply to be able to note down references to parts of books with precision. […] This reference system, still widely used today for classical texts and poetry, in the Middle Ages did not cross the Channel [...]’ (Authentic Witnesses, 1991, pp. 234-36). The removal of the Bible to Italy shortly after it was produced makes it an interesting witness to the 13th-century movement of books and students between Oxford and Italy, especially within the Dominican order. Sister leaves from this Bible can be identified on the basis of the unusual line-numbering, in which Arabic numerals are used with a more antique counting system (for a full account of this manuscript see: P. Kidd, ‘A Recently Dismembered Illuminated Bible, Probably from Oxford’, https://mssprovenance.blogspot.com/2020/03/a-recently-dismembered-illuminated.html).
provenance: Giacomo Bianconi (1220–1301) (Giacomo Bianconi (1220–1301), founder and prior of the Dominican convent of Bevagna in Umbria); Piasa (Firm) (Piasa, Paris) [ 2007	]

authors: Aristotle (Aristotle); William, of Moerbeke, approximately 1215-1286 (William of Moerbeke (1215-35–c.1286)) [Tr]
manuscript_binding: in a minute, heavily abbreviated calligraphic hand, ruled space: 112 x 76mm., rubrics in red, paraphs alternately in red or blue, penwork initials in red or blue with flourishing of the opposite colour throughout, larger initials opening the Books (lacking opening, and two further leaves after ff.23 and 60, f.32 with a marginal slice in the vellum, once repaired but now missing the repair, edge of f.64 cut away, a few wormholes, especially to flyleaves, occasional staining and smudging but generally in excellent condition). 19th?-century blind-tooled calf, marbled endpapers (edges and spine a little scuffed).
other_info: Manuscripts of Aristotle are extremely rare on the market, especially ones with such impressive institutional provenance as the present copy. The Nicomachean Ethics is widely considered to be one of the most important of philosophical works: in it Aristotle outlines the theory of virtuous character based on the idea of finding a golden mean, along with valuable insights about friendship, courage, generosity and justice. Its influence in the European Middle Ages cannot be overstated, and one of the primary translations of the text was carried out - apparently at the request of Thomas Aquinas - by the Flemish Dominican William of Moerbeke, prolific translator of philosophical, medical and scientific texts. Moerbeke died in c.1286, and the colophon in the present manuscript describes the content as 'nove translationis'.

other_info: fos. 238 + vi. With Parisian Calendar, added mid 13th cent. With additions of late 13th and early 14th centuries. The book was extensively repaired at the edges throughout in the early 14th century, and from the care and skill devoted to the repairs must have been a highly-valued possession. Decorative initials in red and blue pen-work and large initials in gold and colours of early 13th, late 13th and early 14th centuries. Miniature of the Crucifixion with seven saints, and one historiated initial of priest celebrating Mass, both with bar borders and ivy leaf decoration, added c. 1340, at the Canon of the Mass. He acquired it in 1922 in two separate portions, A, of 186 leaves, and B, of 52 leaves. other_info: The rich illumination of this Breviary signals a luxury production, and it appears to have belonged to, or was made for, an Augustinian friar in Lyon.  Recitation of the text of the Breviary – the Divine Office centering on the Psalms – was at the heart of the religious life of monks, nuns, and friars; that the present volume is illuminated (by the workshop of the little-known Master of the Vienna Roman de la Rose) suggests that the friar-owner either came from wealth or received the manuscript as a gift from an affluent donor.  Features of its calendar, text, and iconography all merit closer study.

manuscript_binding: Legatura pergamena
other_info: [...] una grande miniatura (cm. 12 x 7); 10 ricchissime cornici a pagina intera, numerosissime iniziali miniate e dorate [...] c. 2 v. (guardia) i prolegomeni del calendario: Exclamant tristes indumentis spoliati / Lugent penitentes letantur glorificati. Seguono altri tre versi [...] Nel lato destro della stessa c. un quadrante o gnome cronologico con la data del 1468; c. 3 r. : comincia il calendario; attorno alla pagina una ricchissima cornice [...]; in alto: Januarius habet  dies XXXI; seguono altre 5 carte per il calendario (in tutto sono sei e ogni mese occupa una faciata) scritte con inchiostri di vario colore e lumeggiate di piccoli e grandi iniziali miniate. In principio ogni mese (salvo genaio) un verso a rime leonine che indica l'influenza nefasta di due giorni per ciascun mese: Fevrier: Quarta subiit mortem prosternit tertia fortem / Mars: Primus mandatentem disrumpit quarta bibentem / etc. [...] c. 10 r. : un bel fregio laterale; un bastone sormontato di una corona e nel margine superiore e inferiore, per tutta la larghezza della prima colonna, arabeschi e fogliami:  Ce sont les segres des Dames translates de latin en fransois mes il sont defandus de rever (sic) a fame par nostre Sainct pere le pape sus peine descomuniement en la decretal ad meam doctrinam. Indi comincia il testo: UNE DAMOISELLE ME PRIA pour loyalle cortoysie que je dictasse ou escripsisse aucune chose proufitable ...  Al principio della 2a col. : Au commenceamant de ce livre devez scavoir et entendre comme une et ung chacun  prant char et commencemant de essence ou estre . Les philosophes dient que chacun tient son estre de la semence du pere et de la mere [...]; c. 15 v. col. 1a, l. 38-41: Item sans peril donez luy a boyre pouldre de yvoyre avec vin blanc et tantost [se] delivera [...] In alto sul margine sinistro della 1a col. di altra mano antica, un elenco de sei specie d'epidemie; nel margine inf. della pag. due note di possesso: Ex libris Guillelmi Innocentii Tolosatis chirurgi 1582. Fuit emptus hic liber in vico portae Arietis 3a maij 1582. stt. - Ex libris Villar Tolosatis professoris chirurgi. 1777. Fuit missus hic liber ad dominum Perysilhe doctorem medicum, necnon almae Academiae parisiensis scocium. 5 ott. 1777 [...] c. 16 r : due cornici  simili a quella della c. 3; in alto, prima colonna, in rosso: In nomine domine Amen. nventarium seu colectarium in arte cyrugicali et medicine cōpletum et cōpilatum. Anno domini milesimo trecentesimo sexagesimo [tertio] per me Guidonem de Galliaco cirugicum et magistrum in medicin [...] Tra l'incipit e la prima parola del testo, una grande miniatura rappresentante un maestro in cattedra, sotto un baldacchino scolpito, mentre legge un libro aperto sul leggìo che gli sta dinanzi  . Ai suoi lati San Cosmo e San Damiano recanti in mano spatola e unguento; a piè della cattedra, seduti su banchi anche scolpiti, quattro discepoli [...] LES SEGRES DES DAMES, che formano la prima parte del nostro codice, sembrano di origine tolosana, a giudicare dalla lista delle feste e dall'elenco dei santi contenuti nel calendario [...] Per la storia esterna del volume aggiungeremo che uscito di Tolosa, esso fu venduto all'asta dal Potier, nel marzo del 1854, e che in quell'epoca fu acquistato dal Dr. Colson. Tav. LVI. [Source for hammer price: 'Notizie', La Bibliofilia, vol. 31, n. 3/4, 1929, p. 171; the estimate in the catalogue was 40,000 Lire]

other_info: Un fleuron gravé, du temps de la Restauration, a été grossièrement appliqué au verso du dernier feuillet, probablement pour faire disparaître les traces du grattage d'une estampille. L'ancienne pagination, marquée par un bibliothécaire de Saint-Victor, a été effacée. L'auteur de la nouvelle pagination a mis en tete du volume (feuillat A) une table des "lays et balades qui ont des titres;" cette table, que M. le marquis de Queux de Saint-Hilaire a reproduite, est datée du 5 juin 1787 et signée "E. Rondeau;" en réalité, cette table doit avoir été écrite vers 1840 ou 1845, avec une date et une signature qui constituent un faux commis pour rendre méconnaissable l'origine du manuscrit. A la fin du volume sont ajoutés 10 feuillets (36-45) sur lesquels on a copié une table et quelques extraits, du temps que le volume appartenait à Barrois.

other_info:
Cursive script; Fol. 1 is lacking; it evidently had a decorated frontispiece and a coat of arms, for such are visible in the lift-off on the verso of the front flyleaf. The sections on paper are not bound in with the vellum leaves, but are two separate additions, of different dimensions: fol. 61-66 (3 nested bifolia, 215 x 150 mm.); fol. 67-72 (2 nested bifolia and 1 separate bifolium, 230 x 165 mm.). The sections on paper contain alphabetical indices to the rubrics of specific texts; the first index does not correspond with the rubrics of this manuscript, but the second index does, indicating the pages each rubric falls on, although the manuscript is foliated; there are watermarks on the paper.

titles: Officium Beatae Mariae Virginis (Book of Hours)
places: Venice, Veneto, Northern Italy, Italy, Europe
other_info:
Italian Book of Hours, c1470-1480, beginning Officium Beatae Mariae Virginis (office of the Blessed Virgin Mary). Originally 106(?) leaves, with 19th-century additions: full page colour illustrations and decorated borders, including a Crucifixion, added by Caleb W Wing.
The manuscript was written by the Venetian scribe Marcus de Cribellariis (or Marco di Vicenza). Additions were made to the manuscript by Caleb W Wing, originally employed c1846 to restore damaged items for John Boykett Jarman, a collector and dealer with premises off Bond Street.
Provenance Notes: The 19th-century additions to the manuscript are thought to have been made while it was in the possession of John Boykett Jarman; bought in the Jarman sale in 1864 by the bookseller Lilly, who sold it to William Bragge of Sheffield; bought by Quaritch at the Bragge sale in 1876, but was returned, probably due to its spurious additions; sold at Sotheby's in 1881 to Alexander, Baron Peckover of Wisbech, whose bookplate is attached to the second end-page (exhibited at the National Exhibition of Works of Art, Leeds, 1868); presented to UCL by Professor L S Penrose, grandson of Alexander, Baron Peckover of Wisbech, in 1949.
Fifty-five leaves containing the penitential psalms in Italian, a litany, and other texts seem to have been originally part of this manuscript. These leaves, written for someone called Evangelista, were in the Celotti sale, 1825, and the Phillipps sale, 1903, in which they were sold to Sir Sydney Cockerell; they later belonged to Mr Brian S Cron.

This is an early work by Battista Agnese (1527–1564), one of the most distinguished sixteenth-century makers of portolans (nautical charts). Agnese’s work represents the late peak of this tradition, in which technical accuracy was matched by artistic skill.
The seven maps (five of which appear to be in Agnese’s own hand; see overleaf) portray Britain and north-west Europe; Spain and North Africa; the Mediterranean (from northern Italy to Antioch); the seas of Marmara and Azov and the Black Sea; the Adriatic; the Aegean; and a world map. The world map includes the Straits of Magellan, discovered in 1520, and seven named towns in North and South America, although the west coast was still unknown at the time it was produced. This, and other inaccuracies which Agnese later corrected, date the atlas to among the first of Agnese’s productions.

other_info: This delightful Italian prayer book has a rich history. Commissioned in the fifteenth century for a young noblewoman, it was later owned by a Dutch merchant living in Venice who used it, in part, to teach his son to read. Written in Italian, the manuscript highlights the growing importance of vernacular texts in fifteenth-century Italy. Finely decorated initials and a frontispiece with a skull on burnished gold add to the manuscript’s luster. Though largely unstudied, vernacular prayer books such as this offer rich literary witness to the practice of lay religion in the late Middle Ages.
